speechtext: for leave to introduce Bill No. C-57, to amend the Criminal Code (capital punishment).

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO ABOLISH CAPITAL PUNISHMENT EXCEPT FOR TREASON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the Criminal Code as it presently stands murder is divided into capital and non-capital classifications, with death being the punishment for capital murder and life imprisonment the punishment for non-capital murder. The purpose of this bill is to provide that, except in cases of treason, the punishment for murder shall be life imprisonment. In short, the purpose is to abolish capital punishment except in cases of treason.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
I regret to inform the house that at approximately 7.50 p.m. yesterday, October 10, a very unfortunate accident occurred at R.C.A.F. station Bagotville, when an R.C.A.F. CF-101B Voodoo aircraft, while taking off on a routine night operation, collided with a T.C.A. Viscount as it was turning off the runway. One member of the T.C.A. crew was killed instantly and one passenger died shortly after being admitted to hospital. The crew of the Voodoo managed to control their aircraft until they could ensure that it would crash in an open field before they ejected at a dangerously low altitude, and with some injury to themselves.
Until such time as a complete and exhaustive investigation has been carried out it will be impossible to determine the exact cause of this accident. Such an investigation was instigated immediately, and the most highly qualified personnel available were flown to the scene within hours. Every facility and assistance are being provided to this team. However, it is not yet possible to forecast when the results of this investigation will be available.
The Department of Transport is co-operating in the investigation.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: LIEFCORT-STATEMENT AS TO COMPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Parkdale asked me a question relating to the composition of liefcort. I am advised that the food and drug directorate was not aware that the dose of estradiol in liefcort was ten times the usually recommend dose. I should point out, however, that much higher doses than the usual dose are given in the treatment of

certain diseases. It was only after an involved chemical analysis that we found it not to be an extract of adrenal glands but a synthetic extract of hormones and hormone-like substances related to the adrenal and sex glands, including estradiol.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, I should like to clarify an answer I gave in the house yesterday on our action in banning the distribution of liefcort. I told the hon. member for Essex East that the food and drug directorate of my department had stopped the distribution of this drug before action had been taken by the United States. In fact I find we acted before the United States food and drug administration let it be known that the drug could not be legally imported into the United States.
The point is that it is illegal for any drug to be imported into that country unless a United States new drug submission has been filed. The United States authorities discovered some time ago that liefcort was crossing the border, and customs officials were alerted automatically to refuse entrance to it. However, these instructions were based on the procedural question I have indicated. When Washington advised my department of the release on Tuesday, I assumed that it coincided with the issuance of instructions to border points.

subtopic: LIEFCORT-STATEMENT AS TO COMPOSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should also like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare with regard to liefcort. Dr. Liefmann has stated that he and his colleagues could continue to use liefcort. Is this in keeping with the order of the food and drug directorate?

speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: LIEFCORT-STATEMENT AS TO COMPOSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a clear distinction must be drawn between medical practice and the manufacture of drugs. While my department does have the right to control a drug under manufacture, it has no power to interfere with a doctor using his medical judgment to give treatment to individual patients. Dr. Liefmann is no longer manufacturing this drug for distribution under any circumstances outside his own office, and that is the only point with which we can be concerned. speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this 25th parliament meets in special circumstances since Canada must face heavier responsibilities.
Personally, I am both pleased and honoured to be able to bring my modest contribution to this task as parliamentary secretary to such an important minister as that of agriculture. To my knowledge, it is the first time that a French Canadian holds such a post for that department in this house. I shall thus have the opportunity of being of greater service to the farmers of my country, to my fellow-citizens in eastern Canada as well as those of my province and of my constituency, who are already assured of my devotion. I have no greater wish than to put the knowledge I have of agronomy and my humble talents at the service of our nation's agriculture and of the development of the area which has done me the honour of re-electing me. Farmers from all across Canada, as well as eastern farmers and especially Quebec farmers, will find that I am ready to listen to their problems and to co-operate.
Although Canada is becoming an industrial power in the world, agriculture remains indeed one of the most vital factors in the Canadian economy. But it is true to say that the number of individuals directly concerned with agriculture has come down in these last few years, although farms are getting larger and production is more and more industrialized.
Agriculture remains the basis of our national economy and the yardstick of our prosperity. But in Quebec, we note with regret that of the 134,000 farms under cultivation in 1950, there were only 122,000 left in 1956 and scarcely 96,000 in 1961. Agriculture has not been too affected however, since farm production has continually gone up. Using new machinery and new methods, our farmers are

more active and our farms more productive.
It cannot be denied that it is the result of the work carried on, during the last few years, by our federal Department of Agriculture, the dedication of our county agronomists, the cooperation of numerous experts and in particular the result of the sustained efforts made by professional associations and co-operatives who lead and support the farmers.
However, in the front rank of these organizations comes our federal Department of Agriculture whose experiments and research benefit the whole country. I will be called upon to work more closely, in the future, with that department and I am proud of it because I will have an opportunity to help implement our Minister of Agriculture's great instructions regarding the marketing of agricultural products, their classification, the health of livestock, the freight subsidy for grains and finally the fine provisions of the Agricultural Stabilization Act. The last report of the stabilization board, which was received a few days ago, shows that more than $126 million were spent on agricultural prices support in Canada and that 18 products of various kinds benefited from it.
In Canada, and especially in our province, the considerable progress already seen is due to an elite of farmers who have been trained by great agronomists and true philosophers of rural thinking.
However, I worry over the fact that most of our family farms are not getting an adequate income. When one thinks that rural life rests first upon the family and then the parish, it is urgent that every endeavour be used to raise the standard of life of our rural families, so that the farming class can enjoy the same benefits and the same privileges as the other social classes.
According to the figures of the 1951 census -those from last year are not yet available- the gross income of more than 50 per cent of farms in the six eastern provinces of the country amounts to less than $2,500. This is absolutely insufficient for the owner or the producer who had to make heavy expenditures to organize his farming operations and who finds himself with a completely inadequate income which prevents him from enjoying a standard of life where he could honourably provide for his family and for the education of his children. This situation exists 27507-3-25J
The Address-Mr. Pigeon mostly in the areas which are called marginal. There might even be some at home.
I firmly intend to use my knowledge and energy to seek a solution which will raise the living standard of our farmers, especially in Quebec. In many cases, our farms are undoubtedly too small to give an adequate yield. We shall very likely have to make full use of our tillable land and industrialize reasonably our farms for the processing of western grain, in order to promote more extensive cattle farming at home.
We shall also have to strive to produce economically feed grain for the production of poultry, hogs and beef, if possible, in the eastern provinces. I am sure that the committee on feed grain will be able to consider this problem with the co-operation of the Canadian wheat board. This problem is of particular interest to me.
Other marginal areas will need additional assistance, and I believe that the legislation adopted some time ago under the name of Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act, better known as ARDA, can bring a solution to this problem.
This legislation can become a vital instrument in these areas, either by promoting certain specialized crops, the development of co-operatives and local industries, the grouping of certain operations, reforestation, and the rest. The act permits use of the knowledge, energies and goodwill of all those who want to contribute to the economical improvement of the less favoured centres. Here again, I find a problem which calls for a solution and I have been working at it for some time.
I should like to point out that, as early as the first of May 1962, the Minister of Agriculture, with whom I have the honour of co-operating presently, sent out to premiers of the provinces an invitation to co-operate with the federal authorities for the implementation of this Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act. For instance, the federal Department of Agriculture is contemplating an assistance of about $10,439,000 for the province of Quebec, over a three year period, $750,000 of which would make up the first payment.
I dare hope that the government of the province of Quebec will sign an agreement on this matter with the federal Minister of Agriculture, at the earliest possible date.

The Address-Mr. Pigeon
ARDA, with the possibilities for action and adjustment it opens, has already been recognized as the legislation of the century. It is a new tool in the hands of men who pride themselves with being modern. Therefore, it is up to us to make use of it so as to give better service to the people.
May I now quote a few thoughts expressed by the minister Edgar Pisani, of France:
Since we are swept along, rivalled and buffeted by civilizations opposed to ours, it is our duty to give to all men mastery over their trade, the capacity to organize their efforts concerning their industry and to bind them to a civilization of which they are the trustees, the beneficiaries and the guardians. Each farmer must be given mastery over all that, if not, we will have failed in our task, which is to give everyone a hope, everyone a future.
We earnestly wish that the provinces will agree to implement that important piece of legislation.
Allow me to point out the benefits which have accrued to Canadian dairy producers since the support price on butter has been increased from 58 cents to 64 cents a pound, that is a supplementary increase of 6 cents a pound, from May 1958 to September 1962. Total production during that period amounted to 1,633,901,000 pounds. If we add to that amount the estimated production, from September to December 1962, that is 108 million pounds, the total amount would reach more than $98 million. That additional income is, therefore, what Canadian farmers have gained and will gain, for butter production, on account of the increase in the support price from 58 cents to 64 cents at the end of December 1962. To that might be added the fact that all Canadian producers of milk, to be processed for purposes other than for butter, have also benefited from an increase of about 25 cents per hundred pounds for their milk, either for the production of cheese, concentrated milk or other concentrated products, there again about $12 million a year.
May I emphasize that the provinces alone have the right to legislate in connection with the sale of dairy products within their respective territory. To that effect, all provinces- except Newfoundland-have a provincial milk board. These boards determine milk prices paid to the producers for the sale of non-processed milk on the public market. Minimum prices for milk producers selling their non-processed milk to the consumers have been established, and several provinces have


even established minimum prices per quart to be paid by the consumer.
Mr. Speaker, some provinces have entered into an agreement with Ottawa in order to implement our excellent federal crop insurance act. It is quite pointless for us to wait for a reply from the Quebec department of agriculture, which would allow farmers of that province, especially those who are engaged in specialized farming, to benefit from the advantages of that act. The federal government is prepared to pay 20 per cent of the cost of premiums and 50 per cent of the administrative cost of that act.
Mr. Speaker, it is probably as a result of the excellent farm policy of the present federal government, as a newspaperman from La Presse wrote on September 25, that:
Quebec farmers prefer to borrow from Ottawa.
The same newspaperman also pointed out the following:
Under the federal-provincial agreement on farm loans, the provincial government grants a 2.5 per cent refund on the 5 per cent interest claimed by Ottawa from borrowers. This means that the rate of interest on federal loans is equal to that of the provincial farm loan board, i.e. 2.5 per cent.
The Quebec government is granting that refund because the provincial farm loan board has run out of funds.
Even if the interest rates are now identical-
The La Presse journalist goes on to say:

what advantage is there for people in Quebec in appealing to the federal government rather than to the provincial government?
To those who ask the question, Ottawa answers that the maximum loan awarded by the federal farm credit corporation is $27,500,
i.e. $12,500 higher than the loan granted by the provincial farm loan board. The large farm owner who wants to modernize his facilities therefore finds it more interesting to borrow a large amount than to ask for a small loan, and that is why he turns to Ottawa.
It is, therefore, not surprising, in order to complete the figures I quoted a moment ago, to hear that the number of loans granted in Quebec this year is about 750 per cent higher than last year, having risen from 109 to more than 800. This is how the federal government helps Quebec farmers.
It should also be pointed out that, for the first time this year, the farm credit corporation published in a single volume a completely bilingual report. This is another gesture in favour of bilingualism on the national level.

With regard to French Canadians, it also seems proper to mention that two of our own people have recently been appointed members of the advisory committee of the agricultural stabilization board. I refer to Mr. Georges E. Turcotte, who has been recently appointed assistant director of the federated co-operative of Quebec, and Mr. Lionel Sorel, deputy president of the catholic farmers' union of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, another achievement of the present government could well, in the long run, become vital for the cause of peace and agriculture in the world. I refer to the development of a world food plan, called for a long time food bank. The purpose of the plan is to achieve a more equitable distribution of the food resources in the world; to put at the disposal of depressed or underdeveloped nations food that the more developed nations sometimes produce with surpluses.
Decisive action along those lines was taken early last month when delegates from some 30 countries met at the United Nations headquarters in New York. It was, as it was called, a subscription conference aimed at raising the necessary funds for the financing of this food plan. In fact, some 20 countries agreed to subscribe the equivalent of about $87 million out of an objective of $100 million. Other contributions will probably come to complete this objective during the next few months, thus getting the plan going on an experimental basis, at first.
Mr. Speaker, this recent conference in New York followed logically the meeting of the FAO held in Rome last fall. At both meetings, the leader of the Canadian group was no other than the present Minister of Agriculture. At both meetings, the minister moved the adoption of measures necessary to ensure a good operation of the plan. On behalf of Canada, the minister pledged, moreover, a financial contribution of $5 million, with a third in cash and two thirds in farm products.
During a recent speech he made in my riding of Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm, the present Minister of Agriculture said unequivocally that the main Canadian contribution to the plan would be in dairy products.
In that respect, I should like to point out that such a plan had been advocated for practically 20 years. The international federation of farm producers had been asking for such a scheme at everyone of its annual meetings.
The Address-Mr. Pigeon So had the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and, by the same token, the catholic farmers' union and the Quebec federated co-operative which automatically support the international federation since they are affiliates.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all my colleagues are just as happy as I am about the fine steps taken and the important appointments made by the present government.
We can only be confident in the future because the speech from the throne pointed out that Canada's crops this year are abundant and of fine quality, and that our foreign markets for agricultural products have greatly improved.
The Department of Agriculture is headed by a very likeable and competent man who fully understands the needs of farmers as I found out.
Mr. Speaker, even though I have been immediately concerned with the affairs of the Department of Agriculture for only a few weeks, I was in a position to realize that some of the recommendations of the Glassco commission are well founded.
I appreciate the aspirations of our ethnical group within the Canadian confederation. In my opinion, the main duty of the Canadian Department of Agriculture, where I shall now be working, is to guide, direct and support the efforts of Canadian farmers. Now, in the province of Quebec and in other areas of the country, in eastern Canada mostly, there is a large group of farmers who want to progress and to bring their contribution to our economy, but who do not speak the language of the majority. Now to guide and manage properly, this department, which is now in command, must have excellent communications with French speaking farmers.
After spending a few weeks in studying the organization of this large department, I feel that improvements would be possible in this field of better communications between this department and our French centres in particular.
I wish to assure the farmers in my province and in other centres of French Canada that I shall make every effort to improve that situation. On that point, I can already count not only on the understanding but also on the full co-operation of the Minister of Agriculture as well as on the co-operation of my colleagues in parliament, especially if

The Address-Mr. Teillet I can show them that everything that could raise the economic level of our people, when they understand better the instructions of our national Department of Agriculture, will help strengthen the whole Canadian economy.

After all, the role of agriculture in Canada is first of all to feed the nation, to feed it well as far as quantity and quality are concerned, and then to do its own share in order to restore the general economy through exports in every available sector.

Let us look at the facts. It is important that these facts be known. This distorted picture has caused such an impression on the people of our urban areas both in western Canada and in eastern Canada that it may become difficult to obtain the assistance that western farmers need. The picture painted will make it look ridiculous when we come to claim needed and justifiable assistance for

western farm communities. With such a rosy picture in the minds of the public generally, how will this government or the Liberal one to follow justify itself when expenditures are required to assist western farm communities?
There are still many things that need doing, and some of these things are referred to in the Liberal policy declaration which was laughed at the other day by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture when he took a document supposedly to be placed on record in Hansard and then proceeded to place on that record only a very small part, and that small part distorted. We may have more to say about that later on.
First let us look at the export record. Here, if the government and the minister concerned had told the whole truth, no one would have been able to criticize too severely. The record for the period of Tory government from 1957 to date is good. In fact it is almost as good as it was in the corresponding period of Liberal administration. That, for a Tory government, is quite an accomplishment. During the years from 1957 to 1962, total exports of grain and grain products amounted to 2,029,560,000 bushels, or an average of 405,900,000 bushels a year for that period of five years. In the corresponding period of five years, 1952-57, the total exports of grain and grain products were, 2,199,503,000 bushels, or an average of
439.900.000	bushels per year. In other words, the Tory record was only 169,932,000 bushels during the period under review, or 33,986,000 bushels average per year less than the previous corresponding Liberal period.
But in all fairness there may have been a good reason for this. Production dropped considerably during the latter half of the period which I am reviewing, and these figures are most interesting. During the previous five years farmers produced in wheat alone
2.760.212.000	bushels, while during the latter period wheat production was 1,922,061,000 bushels. In other words, if the production record had been maintained during the Tory period of this review, we would find an additional 837,151,000 bushels of wheat on hand at the end of the 1961-62 crop year. That, Mr. Speaker, is the complete picture; and incidentally, the figures I have quoted here are from the Canadian wheat board.
Now let us look at the claim "You have never had it so good", and "Farm cash income from farm operations reached an all time high". Mr. Speaker, you will recall that the other day I attempted to have the Prime Minister define what he meant by "cash income" and his attitude to me was "Sit down, little boy. You are new here. Talk when your elders will permit you". And he refused to

answer the question. He said, as reported on page 98 of Hansard:
All I can say is that I think it defines itself for most hon. members.
Well, Mr. Speaker, does it define itself for most hon. members? There is one here to whom it obviously does not. The term "cash income" as used by the wheat board and by the grain trade means "cash received from all farm operations", and is the equivalent of the term "gross income". The Prime Minister's statement is almost correct. The cash income from farm operations in 1961 has been exceeded only twice, and that was in the early fifties. But that is not the point I wish to make. The real point is that that figure of the highest cash income in 1961, according to the Prime Minister, points up the real difficulty of our western farmers. If we add the last half of this story to the first half stated, we then have the whole picture and the whole truth, which is this. During the year when the Prime Minister says that the cash farm income from farm operations was at an all time high, the net income for the farmer-that is, the amount left to him after deducting his costs-was the lowest in ten years. That is the complete story.

At this point I want to appeal to all hon. members of this house to understand that this is the real plight of our farmers in Canada. I trust that hon. members will tell their constituents that our western people are not crying wolf while they are rich and have "never had it so good".
I wonder if the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, who I do not see in his seat, has heard the story going the rounds in Manitoba about the statement by the Minister of Agriculture that the people in the constituency of Brandon-Souris, the constituency of the minister of northern affairs, were so rich that it was impossible to buy an automobile in Brandon, and that they were taken as quickly as they came in. Someone took the trouble to check that, and that story is in the same category as the rest 27507-3-26
The Address-Mr. Teillet of the Conservatives' statements. There are ample automobiles available in Brandon.
Mr. Speaker, there is on this question a most interesting editorial in the Manitoba Co-Operator of September 6 of this year, which I should like to quote at length. The heading of the editorial is "Mr. Hamilton's Prophesies", and the editorial describes the present crop situation as it appeared to the writer. It goes on to say this:
It is true that farmers delivering wheat will benefit initially from the higher prices received at the time of delivery, but this only applies to wheat, and to suggest that farmers will have the opportunity to deliver grain to country elevators in large volume prior to Christmas would be foolish. This means that the grain farmers' income from the sale of cereals will be well distributed over the crop year and controlled by quota regulations. It is possible that there may not be room in country and terminal elevators for all of the anticipated deliverable grain in this crop year. This, however, will be determined by the volume of export business.
The farm organizations, the management of their elevator facilities and the private companies are realistic on this issue and understand it thoroughly. They are not pumping propaganda to incite the layman. In their modesty they refrain completely from predicting big prices that may not be realized. They are well aware that this year's crop may well produce a great variety of grades, and when the final returns are in at the end of the crop year, No. 3 Northern is likely to be the average wheat grade and the average price. The initial price for this grade is $1.42 per bushel basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver, but less than $1.25 per bushel at the average western Canada country elevator point after handling and elevation charges are deducted. Oats will probably average No. 1 Feed or 44 cents per bushel at the average shipping point. Barley will probably average No. 1 Feed and this will fetch a price of 72 cents per bushel at the time of delivery at the average shipping point. There is no responsible grain spokesman in the west, outside of the political field, suggesting that wheat this crop year will approximate $2.00 or oats 90 cents or barley $1.20 a bushel.
Agriculture Minister Hamilton has been enthusiastic enough to do this. To reach the prices he suggests, No. 3 Northern will have to fetch at least another 75 cents a bushel over and above all charges. No. 1 Feed oats will have to realize at least another 46 cents, and No. 1 Feed barley another 48 cents per bushel average for western Canada. Mr. Hamilton is not only doing the west, and the grain farmers in particular, a disfavor by his inappropriate statements, but is giving eastern Canada and the western layman a greatly distorted impression of what is to come out of the west. True, the prospects are optimistic and thoroughly better than a year ago, but Mr. Hamilton's exuberance puts him in the category of being excessively adventurous in his prophesies.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word about crop insurance. The problem of crop insurance, as we see it now in Manitoba, is a relatively simple one. Enough research and experience has been acquired to reach certain conclusions or, to be more accurate, to confirm the conclusions reached when the scheme was first examined. No one today will deny the necessity of a sound crop insurance

The Address-Mr. Teillet scheme. It has become a vital necessity if the farm community is to survive and avoid becoming wards of governments. I have not time to develop this, but I recommend an examination of the crop insurance scheme report in Manitoba, which in effect said that it was not practicable for a province to carry out an insurance scheme on its own.
Then, Mr. Speaker, a crop insurance scheme was set up under a federal act and some test areas, I believe five in number, were set up in Manitoba. So far, of course, less than 10 per cent of our farmers have participated. There seems to be some doubt about things in their minds, and that, of course, is understandable. When the act was put into effect, the basic requirements for the success of such a scheme were overlooked. Federal participation in premium cost was too low, and it left to the province the larger share of the risk.
I believe that the parliamentary assistant made a statement that confirmed this just a moment ago. This is the very area where the resources of the province are too weak to ensure success. In fact the present scheme, if established over the wide area required for full participation, would risk becoming an open end liability for the provinces which would cause them to become bankrupt.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from a speech by the minister of agriculture for Manitoba, which he made to the agricultural bureau of the Winnipeg chamber of commerce and which is reported upon in the Winnipeg Tribune of December 13, 1961, as follows:
Provincial agriculture minister George Hutton has ruled out any expansion in the Manitoba crop insurance program unless the federal government comes up with a better method of backing it.
Tuesday he told the agricultural bureau of the Winnipeg chamber of commerce that crop insurance couldn't be expanded to cover the whole province with the present system of federal guarantees for losses in the scheme.
Unless the federal government makes changes in its crop insurance act all the western provinces, not just Manitoba, could not provide sound crop insurance, the minister said.
In Manitoba another bad crop year could bring losses as high as $30 million In the Insurance scheme, because there could be a large number of applications following this year's drought. This would be a "tidy sum" to dump on the provincial treasury, said Mr. Hutton.
Under the existing agreement with Ottawa, the province pays the first $200,000 in crop insurance liabilities after the premiums collected and the previous year's reserve have been paid out. Then the province can borrow 75 per cent of extra money needed to cover losses from Ottawa. The province floats its own loan for the remaining 25 per cent. "This in effect means that the province has to borrow all the money In the losses", Mr. Hutton said.
The Manitoba government has proposed a new guarantee for the plan under which the federal government would pay for a large part of losses incurred in years when the crop insurance scheme

goes in the red. The federal payment in bad years would be made in exchange for an annual premium paid to Ottawa in both good and bad years.
It is evident, Mr. Speaker, that these people have yet to understand fully the problem with regard to insurance in farm areas. This scheme is not only important in western Canada; it is needed in all parts of the country. The other evening the hon. member for Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes (Mr. Drouin) made quite a point of this, and I suggest to the members of the government that they take a serious look at the matter and make sure that they come up with an adequate scheme.

Our province is prosperous beyond example .. . We are in the full tide of prosperity under the lowest tariff in America.
Consider for a few moments, Mr. Speaker, if you will the problems that face the people of my own constituency of Cape Breton South. We have been plagued now for years with a declining coal industry. Granted, we have closed dozens of mines, but when this government came to power they told us they were going to do something about the problems facing our coal industry. We had a royal commission under Mr. Justice Ivan Rand appointed to investigate the situation. Not only have this government failed to come up with a long term policy to deal with the problems of the coal industry in Nova Scotia, but they have even refused to accept the minimum recommendations of this particular commissioner. He suggested, for example, to the people of Canada that it might be necessary to close three mines in Cape Breton over a five year period and a fourth mine over an additional five year period, for a total of four mine closures in ten years.
What has been the result? With the most recent closure of No. 16 colliery at New Waterford under this Conservative government that promised us a national fuel policy, we have closed three mines in a little over one year. We are threatened with an end of the steel industry on which we depend to a great extent in the province of Nova Scotia. Last winter our people experienced unemployment at the rate of 25 per cent. We will be the first to admit that we have received assistance from this and other federal governments, but the assistance has always been of a temporary, of a stopgap, of an emergency, of a meet each crisis as it comes along, nature. There has been no progress under this Conservative government since 1957 toward a permanent solution of the economic problems of the coal industry in Nova Scotia or the Atlantic provinces in general.
The Minister of Finance, at the time of the closing of No. 16 colliery in New Waterford, in a press release stated that in the opinion of the government it was in the best interests of the Nova Scotia coal industry to close No. 16 colliery. Well, Mr. Speaker, surely this is a fantastic statement. We ask simply, how can a responsible minister of the crown tell
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
us what is in our best interest when he does not have any kind of policy to deal with this particular problem?
It is regrettable, but I think it is also necessary, that we remind members of this house that the right hon. Prime Minister came to our constituency during the last election campaign and he told responsible representatives of the miners, the district executive of the united mine workers of America, that he was not going to turn his back on the miners. The mine eventually closed, and the Prime Minister not only turned his back on the miners but he refused to meet them to discuss the repercussions of this closure. Under no circumstances, should No. 16 colliery have been allowed to close until a definite policy had been established for the coal industry in Nova Scotia and for the Atlantic provinces' economy in general. There has been evidence, and it is unfortunate, of a disturbing lack of planning and decision making, as well as a complete lack of the application of any kind of social philosophy in the present federal government's handling of this situation.
A few moments ago I said that our region was the most retarded in Canada. Thirteen of the 36 surplus manpower areas in Canada are to be found in the Atlantic provinces. We have 10.4 per cent of the population of Canada but only 7.2 per cent of her income. Our average per capita personal income for 1961 was $1,066 as opposed to $1,593 for all Canada. We have experienced consistently higher unemployment than has Canada as a whole. The present situation is further aggravated, though somewhat disguised, as a result of the considerable underemployment in our primary industries. In other words, if I might sum up the situation in the Atlantic provinces, the only prosperity that we have had in that region of Canada since confederation was witnessed during the railroad construction boom prior to the first world war and during both world wars. Certainly these are events to which we cannot look forward in the future with a great deal of anticipation.

In such an environment as this comprehensive program of economic development would bring about, existing industries could be induced to expand and new industries would be attracted into our area. There are those who would question these particular suggestions. There are those who would say, "Don't you understand these are uneconomic proposals you are making?" In reply, Mr. Speaker, I would say that it is not a question of immutable, irrefutable economic principles. We defied the laws of economics when we built this nation, when we decided to enter into confederation, and surely there is sufficient argument for overlooking some economic principles in view of the particular difficulties of this part of Canada.
There are those who will argue that this policy we advocate is far too protective, but in reply we can point to the protection we are already giving to major industries in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Mr. Speaker, prior to the noon recess I was dealing with the various arguments or charges that might be laid against or put forward in opposition to the comprehensive and specific measures which I had introduced to the house and in which

we believe, in the Atlantic provinces, in so far as the economic problems of this region of Canada are concerned. Specifically I was dealing with the second such possible objection, namely that the policies which we propose are perhaps too protective in this day and age.
In addition to what I have already said with regard to this particular criticism, I would simply like to point out that it is essential, in relation to the coal industry of Nova Scotia, that this government or any other federal government provide our coal industry with sufficient financial assistance to make coal competitive with foreign oil in the province of Nova Scotia, to assure that coal will be used as the basic fuel in generating thermal power in that province. If this is not done, then surely we cannot expect the Ontario market to use coal from Nova Scotia, if we are not successful in ensuring that our own local industries do the same.
Third, Mr. Speaker, it might be suggested that these proposals would all be very well and would probably help our situation substantially, but they cost too much money. We say, first of all, that in measuring the cost of the proposals that are necessary in order to deal firmly and finally with the economic rehabilitation of the Atlantic provinces, we must consider the eventual and ultimate social costs involved in the Atlantic provinces if action is not taken today.
Then, Mr. Speaker, we would point to the fact that Canada has already, spent huge sums of money to build her canals and transcontinental railway system, to provide wheat storage for the western farmers, acreage payments, and so on. We would further point out that the tariff system presently operating in Canada, protecting and insuring the life of our central Canadian industries, costs the Canadian taxpayer indirectly, it is estimated, something in the vicinity of $1 billion a year. These same tariff policies have a doubly depressing effect on the producers and consumers in the Atlantic provinces, because they mean our people must buy their products from the high cost, non-competitive industries of central Ontario while these same protected industries are enabled to turn around and buy their raw materials across the border because they can obtain them there more cheaply. This represents double protection for a large part of our Canadian industry.
Fourth, Mr. Speaker, it might be suggested that we are perhaps somewhat naive down in the eastern part of Canada. It might be said, for example, "Well, after all, you decided in 1867 to participate in confederation, and this is the economic price you have to pay for it". We say, no. We say that

the fathers of confederation recognized the economic implications for that part of Canada when confederation took place, and they wisely and justly attempted to provide for the dislocations that were bound to take place as a result of the national development policies adopted in this House of Commons.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, there are those who would say, "well, your program sounds very good; we would like to help you, but this represents state planning". In other words we come back to the old bogeyman that the Tories raised in the last campaign; it is a question of free enterprise versus socialism. This is nonsense, Mr. Speaker. These are the word fighters; these are the labellers who try to criticize and discredit a new idea by labelling it with a name that is unacceptable to the Canadian people. It is not a question of free enterprise versus socialism. It is a question of the old way versus the new way. It is a question of the principles which at one time apparently were successful in Canada, to some extent, as opposed to the new procedures and methods that we must adopt for the future.

Mr. Speaker, upon rising to take part in this debate it is with genuine pleasure that I give you, and through you to Mr. Speaker, my best wishes. It is indeed a pleasure to see two old friends filling such high offices so capably. At this time I would also like to congratulate the hon. member for Waterloo South and the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska on the capable way in which they moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Last Friday night in that sometimes dramatic C.B.C. television show "Viewpoint" the star of the night said that too many of the speeches in the debates on the speech from the throne were nothing but dreary recitations of the virtues of some backwoods constituency. I think it is well that those who spend a great deal of their time in Ottawa-perhaps too much of their time-should hear from time to time of the virtues, the problems and the wishes of these constituencies. I say this because the strength of Canada is nothing more than the aggregate of the strength of those 265 constituencies. A visit to my riding last week end supported and confirmed the wisdom of the course the official opposition are taking to make sure they do not win any of those non-confidence votes they have been bringing with such regularity.
To preface my remarks in this debate, and in order only to demonstrate the interests of my constituents, I should like to discuss briefly the economy of my riding of Simcoe
The Address-Mr. H. E. Smith North. I think every hon. member who sat in the last parliament is well aware that Collingwood is the largest and most important shipbuilding centre on the great lakes. The policies of the Conservative government in the last five years have brought Collingwood to the highest level of activity in its history even higher than during wartime, because shipbuilding is an industry highly productive of jobs. There are few things which the Canadian government could have done to provide more jobs for Canadians than to introduce the system of subsidies for shipyards, and in case anyone should think that only the larger centres have benefited from this policy, let me tell them that is not so. Shipyards large and small across Canada have benefited from our shipbuilding policies.
Along with the shipbuilders and sailors of my riding I look forward to the realization of the promise in the speech from the throne of added protection for Canadian shipping on the great lakes. If we permit foreign ships to carry our cargoes it constitutes just as large a drain on our foreign exchange fund as, for example, the purchase of imported electrical appliances.
I am sorry the hon. member for Davenport is not here in his place, because harsh things have been said by him and to him during this debate. I should like to thank him for the assistance he gave me during my election campaign, when he made something of an issue of the fact that the devaluation policies of the Conservative government were causing an increase in the price of imported electrical appliances. Now in the city of Barrie, in my riding, there is to be found the largest manufacturer of small household appliances in Canada. There are many other factories there making a wide range of household and consumer goods from tires and plastics to tape measures and cosmetics. I can assure this house that the message of the hon. member for Davenport was not lost on those people when election day came around.
It is interesting to see, now, that the hon. member has finally and firmly come down on the side of the angels, and on the side of the Conservatives; because in the last issue of that journal of Liberal opinion the Fundy Fisherman he says that devaluation is a good and necessary thing. I should also like to note that though the majority of our factories are Canadian subsidiaries of United States companies, almost without exception the local management is completely Canadian in viewpoint and directed to the best interests of Canada.
The farmlands of Simcoe county are rich and productive. Indeed, they too might be said to be secondary manufacturers, because much of their products find their way directly

Pork is processed through Canada's first and largest farmer owned packing plant, with its famous Copaco brand products; finished beef is sent to the Toronto stockyards; tobacco is sold in reasonable quantities on the home market; milk goes to Toronto consumers and cream to the many county creameries; fruit and vegetables go directly to the consumer or else to Colling-wood to be packed for domestic or export use.

Conservative policies have been good for the economy of Simcoe North. The farm credit corporation, as far as our farmers are concerned, represents the finest piece of credit legislation ever passed in Canada. In the course of the past year, or a little longer, over 100 farmers have taken advantage of these loans in our area. Their farms are now

efficient and competitive. They are making money. Conservative policies have contributed to the stability of beef and hog markets. Conservative policies have assisted in the orderly marketing of tobacco. I am sure it is unnecessary to remind the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Roxburgh), who this morning was asking a question about export sales of tobacco, that Canada's tobacco farming industry, an industry highly productive of jobs and requiring many man hours of labour, developed under the protection of a substantial tariff. It is an industry whose export future might well be adversely affected by Britain's entry into the common market, or by the United States trade bill.
Sometimes one hears criticism of the government consumer subsidy on butter. I would just make this observation. Many of our smaller farms are still very marginal operations. It would not take too much to drive these farmers from their land, and very often at an age when they are not adaptable to an industrial society. Surely the butter subsidy, when looked at in this light, is not such an ogre as it is sometimes made to appear.
But the greatest boon to Canadian agriculture and to factory productivity has been the reduction in the external value of the Canadian dollar to 92J cents U.S. Its value to the farmers, factories and factory workers cannot be exaggerated. Beef and pork are finding new markets and are more competitive in the U.S. Our fruit and vegetables are given additional protection in Canada, and our canned fruits and vegetables are finding foreign markets. Cherry pie filling, for example, grown and canned in my riding is now being sold in Germany. For those who worry about the infinitely small increase in the price of imported grapefruit, I suggest that they try Georgian bay apple juice. If the beef you buy costs you just a little more, then think of the jobs and spending power which is being provided for Canadians by the increased exports of beef and pork.
Conservative government policies have been good for the factories and the factory workers in Simcoe county. Yesterday the hon. member

The Address-Mr. H. E. Smith
for Vancouver South quoted some export statistics, and the hon. member who has just finished speaking had some statistics concerning the cost of protection to Canada and the Canadian consumer. 1 do not think it is correct to use statistics in this way, because exports and imports must be considered not only in their dollar value, but must be considered in relation to the production of jobs for Canadians. Because I think that is the aim of all policies; it is not the ultimate dollar sales value or the dollars that we import, but the jobs we provide. Also, I feel that the primary and extractive industries no longer provide the best or the most jobs. These are found, in my opinion, in the secondary and service industries; and of course, as I said before, the service industries depend entirely on the productive industries.
A recitation of the policies applied by our government through the industrial development bank would exhaust my time. Factories employing from two to 200 in my riding have benefited. The aggressive sales policies of the Minister of Trade and Commerce have been used to the fullest. Our factories take every opportunity given to them to explore and get into foreign markets. Indeed, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Transport have the stature of heroes in Sim-coe county. Devaluation has provided incentive, protection and job opportunities for the workers. I am sure the hon. member for Davenport, who is so interested in imported electrical appliances, could find all his needs satisfied from the catalogues of Barrie's appliance industries.
Mr. Speaker, the competitive need to find Canadian material resulting from devaluation has been a challenge that our factories are meeting with zest and initiative. New machines are being installed as fast as people can be found to operate them. I will just mention one example. Hardwood flour is a product which I understand is very little else than hardwood sawdust ground very fine and very dry. It is used extensively in the manufacture of certain plastic products, and until now it has been imported into Ontario from Buffalo. Very shortly it will be manufactured and sold in Barrie.
The factories and factory workers in Simcoe county look forward to the tax incentives now proposed for increased production and export, and they will use these incentives to the fullest to increase production and to provide more jobs. They look forward to the change in our export credit legislation as an essential aid to the products which Canada must export if it is to continue to grow.
In the modern world changes in political, economic and trade alignments are inevitable and continuous. In Simcoe North we have
watched the evolution of the European free trade area, called the European common market. Britain's application to join it and its possible effect upon the commonwealth, upon Canada, and upon Simcoe county we have watched with interest. It may be that the European free trade area is best for Europe, and it may be that it is best for Britain. I think that is for the Europeans and the British to decide. I do not think, though, that it is being parochial or narrow to say that our consideration should be directed to what is good for Canada; because it is only by being prosperous that Canada can make an effective contribution to the free world and to the vast underdeveloped and under privileged areas of the world. If the European common market develops on its present lines-and I think at this time it would be only wishful tn inking to suggest that its world outlook will be toward freer world trade-Canada, a country of 18 million people, will lie between two great western trading blocs, the United States with 180 million or more and western Europe with 175 million. It is now that we must speak out and bargain for our essential needs.
Much of Canada's secondary industry was established by the United States to avoid the tariff differential between the British preferential tariff and the most favoured nation tariff, the most favoured nation tariff generally being higher than the British preferential. Many of the Canadian branches of United States factories have been built in Canada to fill, in addition to Canada's domestic requirements, the import needs of Britain, the commonwealth and other countries. It would now appear that the British preferential tariff must disappear if Britain is to enter the E.C.M. United States manufactures would then enter Canada at the same duty rates as British.
Canada's labour costs have gradually grown closer and closer to those of the United States. We in Canada have a high level of social security which is translated into high taxes and directly into production costs. The smaller Canadian market makes other costs higher. Many United States plants near our borders, with subsidiaries presently in Canada, could satisfy the entire Canadian market for some products with only a few extra shifts in their home factories. If the British preferential tariff disappears, is the devaluation of the dollar by itself going to be enough to keep our secondary industry healthy? What incentives will be left for such Canadian development? Are these companies now going to build their factories in Europe and elsewhere? Must we not now look more and more to other parts of the world for markets for the products of our factories? Will the European common

I think they are important, because it is only in the secondary and the service industries that we can supply the needs of our new job seekers and maintain our high material standard of living.
Mr. Speaker, there is much else in the speech from the throne that commends itself to me and to my constituents, but I have limited myself today to those matters of most immediate interest to Simcoe county.

Mr. Speaker, as I rise to take part in this debate in reply to the speech from the throne in the first session of the twenty fifth parliament and begin to apply myself to the discharge of my duties, I should like to express my congratulations to you for having been chosen by the members of this house to be their Speaker. I should also like to congratulate Mr. Deputy Speaker for the confidence that this house has shown in his ability to assist Mr. Speaker. I should like in addition to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I am aware that on this occasion it is the custom for members to reveal some of the interesting features of their constituencies and the needs of their constituents. In the case of my constituency, Parkdale, which is in the western sector of Toronto, I believe these are well known to the older members of the house through the efforts of the illustrious members for that constituency who have preceded me.
To the new members I should like to say that Parkdale is a fair cross section of Canada. In addition to the Anglo Saxons, virtually all nationalities and colours are represented. In the same way as many of our forefathers, some emigrated to this country seeking a better life; some sought adventure, and some came to this country to enjoy our freedom. Having come to this country in large numbers, for the most part under the wise immigration policies of past Liberal administrations, these people have found freedom and a better life. Today they cling very closely to this freedom and better life, and burn with an abiding desire to assist the enslaved peoples in their homelands during their present adversity. It is this devotion to self government and to freedom, exemplified by so many people in my constituency, which in my opinion is the foundation upon which our future hopes for a greater Canada can be built.
Since it is the duty of members of the loyal opposition to oppose, I cannot see how one can have effective opposition without constructive criticism. Yet we have read in the


press and heard from many members of the government that political criticism is an ugly word. In that regard I refer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who recently made the appalling statement that it is unpatriotic to criticize the government. Before we realize it, Mr. Speaker, political criticism may unfortunately be regarded as an un-Canadian activity instead of democracy's greatest safeguard. Nowhere in the world more ardently than in communist Russia and her subjugated countries is the critic considered unpatriotic, a conspirator and one even deserving of death, but in western civilization the traditional attitude is that criticism is an attempt to test whether what is might not be better. Personally I believe that no reform can be achieved and no survival is possible without the freedom of honest and vigorous criticism.
No manipulation of words, Mr. Speaker, no twisted ideas or faulty memories on the part of hon. members opposite can alter the historic fact that when the present Conservative government took office in June, 1957 it did so as the government of a country whose prosperity was never higher, whose prospects were never brighter and whose prestige among the nations of the world was never so great. In the past five years increased taxes, economic stagnation, high levels of unemployment and loss of international prestige have plagued this country. No one with a sense of fairness, therefore, can honestly argue that the present government through its incompetence and ill-timed policies is not responsible for the chaotic condition of the affairs of this country. In view of the present serious and emergency conditions in Canada, it is the right and the duty of all members of the house effectively to criticize the present government so that alternative and remedial measures will be proposed, the remedial measures so eloquently and wisely proposed by the Leader of the Opposition in this house.
I regret to say that the speech from the throne was a complete disappointment to the people of this country. This has been stated many times by the majority of the speakers who have preceded me. As already described, it is filled with many pious platitudes and is not much more than a rehash of things mentioned in previous speeches from the throne. This government had five years and the largest majority in the history of the House of Commons to bring those measures into being, but still the government continues to fail to put forth clear reasons for the cause of the present economic difficulties, and to reveal definite major policies which are aimed to cure this sick economy.

The seriousness of the situation was cleverly played down in the speech from the throne. Burning matters concerning which the government still owes our country an immediate and detailed explanation are absent from the speech from the throne. To solve the problems of chronic unemployment, slow economic growth and the imbalance of international payments the government has nothing substantial to offer.
In my leader's masterful exposition of the failures of the Conservative government the country has learned about the present administration's damaging mismanagement. This house and the country had the right to hear the Leader of the Opposition condemn the deliberate concealment by the government of the perilous financial state in which Canada found itself last spring. Moreover, all responsible members in the opposition appreciated learning in our leader's clear reply the full facts proving the unfair political manoeuvre committed by the Prime Minister and the former minister of finance last June. In his speech the Leader of the Opposition rebuked the thirteenth Prime Minister of Canada, and rightfully so, for contempt of parliament because it was not allowed to convene after the government failed to get a clear mandate from the people. Still worse, the people of Canada and their elected representatives continued to be shamefully ignored when the Prime Minister dared to attend the commonwealth prime ministers' conference in London, and to present his views and ignore ours. The Prime Minister's disgraceful exhibition of bellyaching in London demonstrated his ignorance of the importance of the European common market.
After all the gloom and doom and crying by the Prime Minister at the commonwealth conference, it was refreshing to hear Mr. J. A. Roberts, deputy minister of trade and commerce, tell the members of a Canadian organization in Vancouver last month that Britain's entry into the common market will be far from a disaster for Canada. He predicted that it would provide potential markets for Canadian goods. What a sharp contrast, Mr. Speaker, to the remarks of the spokesmen of this government who have failed to understand the long term implications for this country of the new overseas trade developments. There are a few more burning issues which I should like to bring to the attention of the government during this debate. Last summer this government announced the deferment of pay increases for 50,000 civil servants, explaining that an increase in wages would be inconsistent with the government's austerity program. By this explanation the Conservative government unloaded some of its problems on the backs of a relatively small group of civil servants unable to fight hack strongly. Our country, one of the richest lands on earth, should be able, with a competent government, to easily afford to pay its civil servants decent salaries.
Other categories of citizens who have been neglected by this government are those thrown out of jobs through automation, the sick, and our senior citizens. We on this side of the house welcome the proposal of the Leader of the Opposition to provide an improved retraining program for workers before, not after, losing their jobs. We are proud also that the Liberal party recognizes the urgency of extending family allowances from age 16 to age 21 for all boys and girls attending school.

We welcome too the other points in the Liberal program of social reform which, though it will cost money, will actually be an investment in this country. As explained by the Leader of the Opposition, under conditions of an expanding economy a Liberal government will provide for health care and adequate pensions, which are repeatedly being refused by the present government. In my varied experience as a practitioner of medicine amongst the working people and senior citizens of Toronto, I learned intimately of their needs. I am deeply concerned with the present inadequate health care and social welfare programs.
In order to refresh the memories of hon. members opposite I should like to state that every piece of social legislation on the statute books of Canada today was enacted by a Liberal government. After the economic depression of the 1930's and the crippling war expenditures of the early 1940's, the Liberal government was financially able to embark on a sound, progressive program of health legislation. Beginning in 1948 the national health program provided for hospital construction, medical technicians and public health research, as well as anti-tuberculosis drugs free of charge to patients in sanatoria, and many other items related to general health.
The second phase of the Liberal health plan, from 1955 to 1956, made available to the people of Canada more hospital additions, medical rehabilitation services, radiological services and free Salk vaccine. In April, 1957 the Liberal minister of health and welfare, now the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), steered through parliament the National Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act. This government is to be condemned for failing to implement all the sections of that act, especially the one relating to the cost of diagnostic tests performed on an out-patient basis, the most costly part of health care today. The blame rests mainly on the present minister of health for failing, in his negotiations with the provinces, to insist that the people of Canada receive the benefit of free diagnostic tests when referred to a hospital laboratory by their doctor.
I am proud, Mr. Speaker, of the fact that my party has always been, and still is, in the forefront in dealing with matters of health care. The Liberal health plan for the future will include progressive coverage of doctors' fees, dental care, nursing services, drug bills and sickness insurance, after full consultation with the provinces and with cooperation from the medical profession. This plan is more comprehensive and more realistic than the plan of any other party in this country.

While speaking on matters of health, Mr. Speaker, I must express my disappointment that the government has failed to explain why it discontinued the free mass immunization program against poliomyelitis with existing safe vaccines. Furthermore, we on this side of the house are still waiting for the government's explanation of the delay of three months in taking the drug thalidomide off the market. We sincerely hope that the government will take early action to improve its control not only over drugs but also over food additives and pesticides, for the greater protection of the Canadian people.
Advanced countries like Canada are facing a great challenge in the field of water and air pollution. Disease causing viruses and chemicals are finding their way into the water supplies of our cities. Many new chemical compounds, including pesticides and detergents, used by industry, farmers and housewives contain inert chemicals which cannot be destroyed by germs in the soil or by present sewage disposal techniques, but chemical engineers tell us it is possible to make a detergent that can be broken down by bacterial action. I would like to bring to the attention of the government the fact that west Germany has already passed a law compelling all manufacturers to abandon the use of hard detergents by 1965.
We also need more government assistance to aid municipalities in improving the purity of water; because disease causing viruses, including that of hepatitis, can pass through in water in present sewage treatment plants. These problems are both medical and political, and should be acted upon without delay by a responsible federal government.
In view of the remarks of the hon. members who have preceded me in this debate, and of the remarks I have added, I believe it is clear that in the speech from the throne the real and urgent needs of the Canadian people have been forgotten and the true condition of Canada's economy has not been revealed. Therefore the Conservative administration stands condemned.

I saw the Queen's first minister of the province of Newfoundland use the authority of the Queen's government to suppress freedom of speech in the province of Newfoundland on June 7 of this year. I was at the table at the time. I happened to know of the events leading up to the invitation by the Rotary club to the then minister of finance to address them. The Rotary club of St. John's chose the subject they wanted the minister to speak on at the then minister's insistence.
During the course of the luncheon, Mr. Speaker, as the minister was arranging his notes in preparation for the speech that was about to follow, a messenger made known the presence in the next room, of the premier of the sovereign province of Newfoundland, and he had words to say to the president of that service club. Here is a letter which was written in his own hand to the president of the club:
Dear Sir:	As Rotary club, by permitting a
politician in the midst of an election to speak on a political subject, became a partisan body I have to inform you that the invitation of the government of Newfoundland to a group of Rotarians to be the guests of the government at dinner next week is hereby withdrawn.

provinces, and it was to be quite a large assembly. And the premier was to speak. Mr. Speaker, this was quite a state of affairs. I submit that this has never happened before in the history of this service club, whose distinguished record of providing a platform to speakers on various subjects is well known across the length and breadth of the country. The then minister of finance, realizing the predicament of his host, the president of the Rotary club, and the other officers who were present, offered to acquiesce to this unreasonable demand. Yes, I say unreasonable because he was still Her Majesty's minister of finance for Canada, and not a "Tory politician" from Toronto. The premier of Newfoundland forgot that fact, just like he forgot that he also was still the first minister of Her Majesty's government in Newfoundland. What a pity he forgets that fact too often. As I say, realizing the predicament of his host, the minister decided it would be the better part of valour to acquiesce to this unreasonable demand, and so another messenger was sent to the little adjoining room to tell the premier, who was shaking with rage, that the minister of finance would speak, but not on the subject of the pegging of the dollar which the Rotary club wanted him to speak on. Mr. Speaker, you will understand my apprehension and emotion in this solemn moment when I am rising for my maiden speech in this chamber where so many great men of our history have performed with far greater oratory than I can muster.
Like my distinguished colleagues, Mr. Speaker, may I offer you my most sincere congratulations, on behalf of the people I have the honour of representing in this house and myself, for your election to the office of Speaker of this august assembly.
