Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the best of success to you in the discharge of your exalted duties which are mainly concerned with protecting our parliamentary freedom and our democracy.
Although I disagree with the hon. members for Waterloo South and Nicolet-Yamaska (Messrs. Chaplin and Vincent), the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, about everything they said here, I wish to congratulate both of them for the elegance and the eloquence they showed in the discharge of their task.
It is in our tradition, I believe, that the debate on the address should give an opportunity to the members to speak of their counties and to briefly expose their needs.
Being the representative of a remote region, perhaps more or less known-I might even say, unknown to several of my hon. colleagues-I shall take this opportunity to speak of Bonaventure county.
First I thank my fellow citizens of Bonaventure for the honour they bestowed upon me in choosing me as their spokesman and I thank the honourable leader of the official opposition in the house as well as my colleagues from Quebec, for having thought of the Gaspe peninsula at the very beginning of this session.
Bounded in part by the Matapedia river, in part by the Restigouche river and for the greater part by the Chaleur bay, the constituency of Bonaventure extends from Routhier-ville, in the west, to Gascons, in the east, over a distance of about 150 miles.

The Address-Mr. Bechard
The population of my constituency earns its living with agriculture, fisheries, forestry and the tourist industry which, incidentally, does not seem to have benefited to a great extent from that healthy devaluation of the Canadian dollar, mentioned in the speech from the throne and about which much fuss was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) last Tuesday, in an earnest effort to explain that urgent measure-a pre-election measure in this case-because never, in the touristic lifetime of the Gaspe peninsula, has there been such a decrease in the number of American tourists than during the summer of 1962.
My constituency is in one of those areas of the country that can be considered as being economically underdeveloped, on account of its remoteness from the larger centres and the prohibitive cost of electricity, an essential factor in the establishment of the manufacturing industries in our area. The result is, and more than elsewhere I think, a frightful and continuous increase in unemployment.
Agriculture being one of the main sources of income in the constituency of Bonaventure and since-
The prosperity of agriculture remains essential to the well-being of the entire Canadian economy.
-as can be read in the speech from the throne, I should like to draw the attention of the house to the outstanding importance which must be given to agriculture in the province of Quebec, and in the Gaspe peninsula in particular, to that sector which I consider as the basis of Canadian economy, if we want to save it.
The high-sounding words uttered and the sensational tricks performed in this house will not make us forget, in Quebec, in the Gaspe peninsula, that the famous post-elec-tional austerity program (so-called urgency measure) in the field of agriculture seems to have been invented, created and brought into the world by the government to "austerize", ostracize and penalize the farmers of the province of Quebec. I shall come back to that in a moment.
Our Gaspe farmers and, I might say, most of our eastern Quebec farmers are complaining that they cannot live on their farms, on account of the lack of development of the land, the lack of marketing organization for the sale of our farm products, which would allow us to sell and consume in this country our own products; in other words, on account of the lack of a farm policy really conceived in the interest of the farmer. Why in the world could we not produce in this country what we can consume in the matter of farm products? According to experts, we have in the Gaspe peninsula the best climate perhaps in Canada for general farming.

However, in view of the prohibitive price of manure and fertilizers, the distance between us and our sources of supply, which increases even more the cost of those products essential to the economical development of our lands, our farmers cannot see when their lot will improve.
Most of those who are still interested in farming, are crushed, overcome, burdened by an enormous debt incurred in buying farm machinery, and which they cannot pay back because the land, insufficiently prepared, will not yield enough to enable them to meet their numerous responsibilities. The result is an abnormal situation, where our farmers are obliged to look for work, in the bush or elsewhere, in order to earn the extra money, if not all the money, they need to pay for their machinery. In my opinion, that does not make sense. A man is a farmer or a lumberjack. He cannot and must not be both at the same time, if he wants to succeed in one field or the other. Not to mention the fact that the farmers who are thus compelled to join the labour force add to the number of unemployed by taking the jobs of available workers. We are making the same mistake again in the field of agriculture, we are putting the cart before the horse. Allow me to explain. The Canadian government is much more favourable to the granting of loans when they are used for the purchase of machinery and equipment than when they are used to improve the land.
To support this statement, I should like at this time to refer to the speech delivered here this morning by the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon) when he stated that when Quebec farmers want to improve their farms by buying machinery and want to pay off debts they have incurred through such purchases and which can amount to $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000, they address themselves to the central government. On the other hand, the provincial government is more concerned with land than with machinery; land comes first, equipment after. And it is the land which should be tackled first, so that it may produce. Then-and only then-shall we think of farm market organizations and farm mechanization. Our local market, if well organized, is able to absorb all that our farmers can produce, and even more.
Without a domestic market, it is useless to think of a progressive development in agriculture. To promote marketing, our farmers must be sure to have, during the off-season, a stock of those products which are most in demand. To this end they must have storage

facilities here and there, grouping various neighbouring communities. There is, in this case, a federal-provincial arrangement to help the farmers build such storage facilities which is, at least, accepted in the province of Quebec. Already, in my county, localities where the establishment of such facilities would be appropriate have been approached, and construction should begin during the summer.
Unfortunately, austerity on the part of this government-the austerity program decreed after the election without any previous consultation of this parliament-a procedure I heartily disapprove, because it is contrary to the most elementary observance of constitutional principles-this austerity program came into being, as I say, to paralyse at home, in Bonaventure, and all over the province of Quebec, the introduction of the policy advocated by the government of Quebec.
It could really be said, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister conceived that emergency program especially to counteract the plans of Quebec farmers.
On the other hand I am told that farmers in the province of Quebec will, because of this austerity program (this so-called emergency measure) be deprived of approximately $1,200,000, which were to be paid out to those who use lime on their farms. Statistics reveal that Quebec farmers use more lime than the farmers of all other Canadian provinces together, and the disappearance of that subsidy is therefore causing to the Quebec farmers considerable injury.
The farmer is furthermore the victim of that same austerity program in that the premium for grade A hogs was lowered from $3 previously to $1, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) having, in addition blotted out the grade B. I was unofficially told that changes have recently been made or will shortly be made to the scheme for grain transportation from western Canada to eastern Canada, which will again bring about a loss of $10 million to the farmers of the province of Quebec.
As far as my constituency of Bonaventure in particular is concerned, I must say that we have there, at Caplan, an experimental farm which gave valuable help to farmers of the Gaspe peninsula.
However, according to a rumour that started going round last winter and is getting stronger all the time, the experimental farm established in my riding by the Liberal government which preceded the present government, is likely to disappear. Therefore, I strongly urge the government, the Minister of Agriculture, to prevent such a disaster from happening in our province, to stop such an injustice while there is still time. It is all very well to say that everybody must tighten
The Address-Mr. Bechard their belts and do their share in these times of austerity; but for goodness sake, do not always take it out on the same people.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate you on your appointment to that lofty seat where you will preside over this house. I am sure all hon. members of this house wish you the very best in an office which will require a great deal of sagacity and wisdom at all times. I should also be remiss if 1 did not congratulate the mover and seconder of the speech from the throne. I thought that they made excellent speeches. As I have looked around and seen so many speakers making their speeches without reading them, I must offer the comment that at no time have I noticed in this house so many speeches given off the cuff and with as few references and as little reading as on this debate in reply to the speech from the throne.
I think that by now it has been proven beyond peradventure that the period of economic crises in this country developed in the few short weeks before the election. Again, I do not want to belabour this point, but I think I should draw attention to the fact that the dominion bureau of statistics issued a report on the flow of capital from this country in the period April 1, 1962 to June 30, 1962. Dissolution of parliament was on April 21 and election day was on June 18.

The Address-Mr. Rynard The report shows very definitely that during this period $300 million went out of this country as interest on investments in Canada. There was a net outflow of short term capital totalling $168 million. But $242 million was invested abroad by Canadians in foreign banks and short term securities, be it noted, and $77 million was spent on travel abroad by Canadians, foreign shipping, and other intangibles. In all, the sum total was $1 billion. That, Mr. Speaker, represents $10 million every day for that 100-day period. What were the causes of this? Various causes have been ascribed but I think the first thing we must look at is the lack of capital coming from the United States. The United States was looking across the ocean to Great Britain's entrance into the common market. The United States was looking for investment there where labour is cheaper and where investment would yield bigger returns. The second point was the $242 million which was invested outside of Canada by Canadians. In my view full credit for that should go to the Liberal party and I think they must accept that.
I want to speak for a minute or two on the devaluation of the dollar. I think the pegging of the dollar was a most courageous step. It was something that had been asked for over a period of years because businessmen knew what the situation would be if we were tied to a dollar that was stable and not fluctuating. They welcomed it. It allowed them to do business and know the price. I could go on and say more about the history of what France and other countries did in that regard but I do not think that is necessary.
I wish to dwell for a minute or two on the effect on my riding of devaluation of the dollar. I represent the riding of Simcoe East which has water on three sides. It is one of the greatest tourist areas in Canada and those in that industry have all experienced a great boom. Practically all of the hotels and summer places were filled at the beginning of the third quarter of the year, the season when the industry experiences a big boost. I want to give all credit to the government in that regard because income from the tourist industry is going to be up $150 million or $160 million. The industry has shown a deficit for years but this year Canada will likely break even. This is due to the courageous action of the government in pegging the dollar.
But I want to go a little further and point out how farsighted the government has been with respect to the tourist industry. Government support of the tourist industry has increased by 75 per cent since 1957 when the Conservative government came into power. Let us compare this with the situation formerly. In the five years from 1952 to 1957


the tourist budget increased by less than 30 per cent but now we see a great increase in the tourist industry in my riding and all across Canada. The Canadian economy has benefited from the increase in income from tourists brought about as a result of aggressive tourist promotion. From 1957 to 1961 income from the tourist industry increased by 30 per cent, or $110 million, while from 1952 to 1956 the growth was 22 per cent or $62 million. Federal programs that have been carried out have laid the foundation for this increase and the pegging of the dollar gave the industry a shot in the arm in every province in Canada. People engaged in the tourist business realize this and they appreciate what this government has done.
I should like to speak for a moment on medical care. Important and all as medical care is, perhaps we in this house would have to agree that food is more essential. Yet food is still bought and sold in the market place. But medical care seems to have something magnetic about it for the politicians. I wonder how much of this is deep concern for the people's welfare and how much of it is concern for the politicians' welfare? I am not going to answer that question. I am going to leave it alone and let hon. members answer it according to their own consciences. Suffice it to say that Liberal policy over the years has been to advocate medical care and forget it as the seasons change. I well remember when they first advocated it away back in 1919. Now, however, since they appear to be swinging far out into left field, they trot it out again in spite of the fact-I wonder sometimes how short their memories are-that very recently they opposed it in the province of Saskatchewan.
One would think that the socialists here would heed the warning to go slow after the medical crisis they precipitated in the province of Saskatchewan. There is no crisis in medical care in Canada. No one is being denied medical care. As a matter of fact, the Ontario hospital commission report indicates that less than 10 per cent need help in this province. They include the indigents and those with marginally low incomes. No one denies that this group needs coverage by insurance or some other plan. As for the remaining 90 per cent, an increasing majority are becoming insured under P.S.I., Associated Medical Services, Windsor Medical Services and other insurance coverage. So I state that this government is taking a very sensible position in having a royal commission bring in a report on medical care.
Canada is a big country. From the Atlantic to the Pacific conditions vary immensely. They vary immensely in Ontario from the

city ol Toronto to the northern part of the province. No physician objects to insurance against sickness. Most of us practise under it now, but we want no interference with freedom of action according to our consciences in treating the patient. That is the way most doctors want things and, let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that is the way most patients want them.

In this way the patient will receive as good treatment as is obtainable anywhere in the world. Furthermore, under this plan it is my firm conviction that no insurance company or group should have a monopoly so far as insurance is concerned.
In my opinion there are a couple of factors that are urgent. I want to bring it to the attention of the house that these are urgent needs. We urgently need more hospital beds, active, convalescent and chronic, in the province of Ontario and throughout Canada. Once we get more chronic beds we can relieve the convalescent, and more convalescent beds will result in relieving the active. But we are in dire need today of active hospital beds, convalescent beds and chronic beds before medical services can be improved. Staffs are urgently needed to man these hospitals. Nurses and other help are required. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that if we did not have married nurses giving of their time and effort we could not operate the hospitals that are operating in Canada today, and may I say that to do so I know some of these nurses have made a great sacrifice so far as their homes are concerned.
Then, Mr. Speaker, I want to draw your attention to the fact that we urgently need more doctors in Canada. The situation is bad, indeed; but it will be worse because the United Kingdom is getting short of doctors today, and that source will dry up. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that a new medical school is needed in this province to provide 100 doctors more per year. It is estimated that the basic science buildings, the hospital and technical buildings for such a school will cost well over $40 million. The need for doctors is urgent because without them no plan of medical care can be carried out. There is urgent need for more hospitals, more staffs and more doctors. These are the urgent medical problems before the people of Canada today. When I say "staffs" I refer to the technicians, radiologists and personnel staff.
Then, I wanted to dwell for a moment or two on the question of welfare payments. I noticed a reference in the speech from the throne to the fact that a welfare council would
The Address-Mr. Rynard be set up to review welfare and social payments. This, in my opinion, is an excellent idea. This matter should be taken out of the hands of the politicians entirely, in my opinion, and these payments should be tied to the economic factors operating in our country. For far too long, the politicians have gone across this country, if not entirely misleading the people, at least attempting to bribe them with their own money.

Shades of 1962.
I should like to discuss briefly the common market situation. First of all, as a Canadian, I regretted reading the comments that were being reported from the Leader of the Opposition. It is my feeling that when the Prime Minister of this country is engaged outside of this country, whether he is a Liberal or a Conservative, his position should not be weakened by irresponsible comments. He is there representing all Canadians and, in my opinion, he is entitled to the support of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. He should not be hampered and hamstrung or belittled at home and reported at home as doing the wrong thing.
The Prime Minister of Canada, the senior member of the commonwealth, occupied a place of respect and dignity in the commonwealth meetings. Of course, he was the first speaker. Not one country questioned the right of the United Kingdom to go into the common market. The United Kingdom negotiations up to this point had been meagre. Only the African nations had been promised associate membership. No arrangements had been considered for Canada's wheat or the other goods that were traditionally sold to England. Little or no discussion had taken place regarding Australia's goods or those of New Zealand, and New Zealand has been the farm basket of the United Kingdom for years. We recall that Mr. Duncan Sandys assured the Australian cabinet less than a year ago that the United Kingdom would never go into Europe unless satisfactory arrangements could be made for Australia. The chancellor of the exchequer had said that the signing of the treaty of Rome would mean having common external tariffs which, in turn, would mean the end of the commonwealth free entry, and he could not conceive of any government of his country putting forward a proposition which would involve the abandonment of commonwealth free entry. However, little or nothing had been done regarding Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India or Pakistan.
There were traditions in that room where these meetings were held. Twenty two years ago the commonwealth stood alone for civilization. Many of these countries had been through two world wars. The question arose,

The Address-Mr. Rynard would the United Kingdom become greater as the leader of a quarter of the world's people, five sixths of whom are coloured, with different religions and different ideals than we have but with great supplies of raw materials and few skills strengthened by over 100 million of the white group. We have Canada coming to the rescue of the United Kingdom in the war and post-war years with $2 billion of help. Canada has supplied the finest wheat in the world to the United Kingdom over the years. Canada buys $2 worth of supplies for every $1 worth the United Kingdom buys in Canada. Ten Canadians visit the United Kingdom for every person who comes to Canada from the United Kingdom. Canada has more than upheld her end in so far as trade is concerned.
To reiterate, perhaps the United Kingdom, with over 100 million whites in the commonwealth, could be a power that would greatly enrich the free world. The Prime Minister's proposal that there be a meeting of all commonwealth members, the common market countries, the United States, Japan and like-minded countries, was a good one. He graciously offered to play host for this meeting. I should like now to quote the following from Canadian Saturday Night:
It was Diefenbaker's finest hour.
To say that his address was deplorable, as Lester Pearson did, shows a complete lack of understanding of the situation which exists in Britain today. Opposition to the common market is growing rapidly, and it appears extremely unlikely that Macmillan will be able to push through his plans. The representatives of the dominions were wheedled back into line by Macmillan, Sandys and Heath, but their endorsement of the vaguely worded memorandum supporting Britain's stand could not be construed as giving the British government carte blanche. The dominions have not had their final say. Nor have the British people.
Now I want to say a few words about the growing viciousness in public life. It is my opinion that a political conscience must be developed if democracy is to function or continue to function in Canada. Downgrading personal attacks and vilification of the Prime Minister of this country, regardless of his political stripe, are wholly unwarranted and unjustified. They create, in my opinion, a lack of respect for the recognized authority of government and debase the character of Canada. They also tend to dilute the political fervour and love of one's country, an atmosphere that is so necessary to developing young Canadians if we ever want them to reach their potential, whatever their avocation may be.
If these scurrilous, unjustified and untrue attacks keep on developing in the trend indicated, then very few men of high calibre will be seeking public office. I am not saying that leaders in public life should be above criticism. They must accept criticism, which

is the essence of politics and political life. However, let us make it constructive. There is no place for destructive criticism or vilification in a country so dependent on exporting 30 per cent of its goods and on the importation of foreign capital to develop its resources fully. Note of this was made by the daily newspaper in my hometown of Orillia.
This paper was founded by Mr. C. H. Hale, who still lives in the city, and who is recognized as a great citizen and newspaper publisher. In fact his contribution to newspaper publication was recognized by the University of Toronto in conferring a doctor of laws degree upon him. His newspaper was finally purchased by the Thomson interests. Mr. Farmer Tissington, now in the press gallery took over. He was already on the staff and he carried on the newspaper with the same high sense of responsibility that was characteristic of Mr. Hale. Then Mr. Tissington went to the Thomson chain at Prince Albert and Mr. James Lamb became publisher, with Mr. Peters as editor. The newspaper's high sense of responsibility to its readers has continued, and I would be most remiss if I did not mention one of the very fine columns contributed to it by Mr. Patrick Nicholson from the parliamentary press gallery. It is from this same newspaper, the Orillia Packet and Times, that I wish to quote an editorial in its issue of September 22:
In the magazine and radio-T.V. field, the grounds are somewhat different. Most of the so-called political commentators who give magazines like Macleans, Saturday Night and Canadian Commentator, and all C.B.C. public forum and political comment programs such a decided leftish slant, are drawn from the same handful of left-wingers whose views range from parlor pink to the sort of fuzzy idealism which is almost a Canadian trademark. To such men Mr. Diefenbaker, with his forthright views, portentous manner and authoritarian leanings is anathema; it is impossible for such men to write objectively of him.
The editorial goes on to state:
Whatever his limitations, and they are not nearly so many or so marked as his critics would have us believe, history will show Mr. Diefenbaker to have been one of this young nation's ablest leaders. He took office at a time when the Liberals openly admitted they were pleased to get out from under, at a time of apparent economic crisis. His government has introduced a host of measures which have improved the condition of most Canadians, and when the economy was again threatened, he did not hesitate to adopt measures which are proving themselves completely successful.
On his record he merits the respect of Canadians of all political persuasions. The bitter and unwarranted campaign of hatred and ridicule to which he is currently being subjected does not reflect credit on many of Canada's political commentators.
While attending the commonwealth prime ministers' conference Mr. Diefenbaker spoke to the Canadian club in London. I wish, Mr. Speaker, you could have been there. It is one

of the biggest halls I have ever been in, and he delivered a great speech there. He made no reference to the scurrilous attacks being made on him back home, but he built up Canada. Had you been there, Mr. Speaker, you would have been proud to be a Canadian. He stood and spoke to that vast audience on an ankle which could not help but be giving him misery. It was his task to build Canada up, and he did.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to avail myself of this opportunity to congratulate you on the honour done you in your appointment to the responsible position of Speaker of the House of Commons. I should also like to congratulate the Deputy Speaker on his appointment, and I would be remiss if I did not compliment the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As a new member I can truly appreciate what an honour it must have been to the two gentlemen concerned and the satisfaction they must feel in having discharged their duty admirably.
The particular aspects of the speeches which followed the speech from the throne which I desire to discuss are those dealing with the unemployment situation generally, the social welfare program of my party, and observations I have to make with respect to the position taken by the other minority parties, particularly that taken by our friends of the New Democratic party.
On the question of unemployment a brief descriptive background of the character of my riding would shed some enlightenment on my primary concern with this question. It is a riding comprising the industrial heart of Hamilton and also, though to a somewhat lesser degree, the industrial heart of Canada. Undeniably it constitutes the steel hub of Canada. Within its boundaries are situated many major industries such as the Steel Company of Canada, Dominion Foundries and Steel, the International Harvester Corporation, Studebaker Corporation, Westinghouse and Dominion Glass, to mention only a few. Thus it can be readily seen it is an industrial riding comprising to a great extent constituents who earn their livelihood through industrial labour.
The continuity of work undertaken by these firms is of vital concern, not only to their employees but to all the people. A slowdown of production or the closing of a particular phase of a productive process reflects on the success of all those whose earnings are of a derivative nature. The small businessman, the man who provides a service, be it professional or otherwise, is deeply concerned with the degree of success enjoyed by these plants.
The Address-Mr. Munro
If one or more of these concerns experience difficulty, whether it be a shortage of work resulting in lay-offs, or whether it be strikes, the ill effects which result reverberate throughout the riding, and indeed throughout the whole city.
One cannot enjoy the confidence of the constituents of such a riding without being in deep sympathy with any policy, policies or party which espouses and embraces this primary premise, namely the betterment of those groups of our citizens who earn their living through physical labour of one form or another. One must realize that the security afforded by continuity of earning power can never be taken for granted by such men. That security is of a far more tenuous nature than one would imagine.
For example, look at the industrial worker. A change in government policy or a change in company policy such as the relocation of one particular phase of its operation, or a slowdown in demand for the company's products, or automation, may result in sudden unemployment with truly grievous consequences not only to the confidence such men have in their country and in our way of life, but even more grievously in the resulting effects of loss of confidence in themselves, irreparable damage to their pride, and damage to the so important and essential belief of Canadians in their own independence and self-reliance, to say nothing of the accompanying hardship which results to the family of an industrial worker when he experiences sudden unemployment. His is a family who do not deserve to suffer, a family who deserve, in a country such as ours, all the essential benefits like proper shelter, nourishment and education. That such essential benefits should be so completely predicated on the constant employment of the breadwinner is a thing which should give us all cause to reflect. Unemployment insurance is but small alleviation for such a devastating toll.
This picture is further aggravated by the fact that an industrial centre such as Hamilton is a focal point in the settlement of many recent arrivals to this country, and without adequacy of employment opportunities these people become disillusioned with the capabilities of this, their new country. This initial disillusionment is hardly a healthy initiation into what we regard as our Canadian way of life.
Unemployment is a serious situation in the country. It is reflected in the city of Hamilton today and can be readily ascertained by an examination of the following facts. First, in the month of July, 1961 there were over 7,000 on the relief rolls of the city of Hamilton; this in the supposed peak of our employment

The Address-Mr. Munro period. This does not even take into account all those unemployed persons receiving unemployment insurance benefits. The bill for providing this very necessary relief was over $3 million for the year 1961, over $1 million of which had to be borne by the city.
Second, home construction is presently grinding to a stop, with the resulting unemployment of contractors, labourers and tradesmen of all manner and kind. Third, lay-offs have occurred and are occurring in our principal industries. The monumental failure of this government to take any constructive measures since it first obtained office in 1957 has been amply dealt with since the opening of this session. Needless to say, the lack of any co-ordinated plan for future economic development, the tight money policy of the present government, with its accompanying high interest rates and the abandonment of many public works, are retrograde steps and ones which will only have a tendency to increase this unemployment which plagues our country. Yet this is the party that held out such radiant hope to the people of this country that the plague of unemployment would no longer visit our land.
The inadequacies of the Conservative government have been so thoroughly dealt with in this house that I think this would be an opportune time to look at the position of the New Democratic party in relation to government policy. May I say now that I share the respect of hon. members for the many distinguished and able men of that group, many of whom have proved themselves, in every type of forum, able and articulate debaters.
Their repeated utterances in this house, however, would lead one to believe that only they, fully and sincerely, reflect the aspirations of the Canadian people; that only they embrace the social ideals so necessary for those Canadians who do not share to a sufficient degree the wealth of this country. Their somewhat sanctimonious attitude would seem to pre-empt all the political virtues unto themselves, to the exclusion of all others. This attitude can, and does, become tiresome. It would lead one to believe that they and they alone are solely fit to carry the torch on behalf of those people who do not adequately share in our abundance, that they and they alone are the sole proprietors of political morality. So jealous do they appear at times that one might even suspect that they resent the fact that any adherent of any other organization or group, be it political or otherwise, might desire to champion the cause or causes which they, our friends, have appropriated unto themselves.
The record of my party in the field of social welfare has been a constructive and

tangible one over the years, and one of which I, as a Liberal, am justly proud. To name only a few: veterans allowance legislation, family allowance legislation, allowances for the blind legislation, old age pensions legislation, phase
1	of the hospitalization plan and in 1956 phase
2	of the hospitalization plan. This only mentions a few. The Liberal party, over the objections of some in this house, were the party that actually implemented this social welfare legislation which is so integral a part of our everyday life today.
Yet were one to read the text entitled "The New Party", the author of which is the hon. member from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and were one to be unfamiliar with Canadian history, I am sure he would come to no other conclusion than that the C.C.F. party formed a government in this Canada of ours during the years in which this social legislation was implemented.
Mr. Speaker, I would quote a paragraph from page 12 of that text as a leading example of a tendency toward plagiarism indulged in by the hon. member from Winnipeg North Centre. It is as follows:
It is generally known that old age pensions were first enacted in Canada in 1926 and that this important social advance was achieved then only because J. S. Woodsworth and a few colleagues held the balance of power in the House of Commons. It is also generally known that the promise to bring in old age pensions had been made by the Liberal party at its convention of 1919.
That last sentence, Mr. Speaker, would seem to be a half-hearted endeavour by the hon. member from Winnipeg North Centre to be objective. Yet to involve oneself in a dispute as to who was the initial author and as to who first implemented such legislation that is so widely accepted today is a childlike discussion. It would then appear that both parties are grappling for the handle of the torch of social change. It would leave one with the distasteful thought that the two parties are more concerned as to who is to acquire the most progressive public image than in a true implementation of the policies necessary to bring about a greater degree of social justice in this country.
I have heard with interest the comments made by the hon. member from York South (Mr. Lewis) and others of his party in their addresses following the speech from the throne. The comments I am referring to are those dealing with the Liberal party, many of which I consider of questionable accuracy. A few examples would be the following. The hon. member from York South stated:
I have noticed in recent speeches by spokesmen for the Liberal party that they too say their goal is a balanced budget. I urge this house to reject this outmoded and harmful proposition at this time.

Mr. Speaker, the actual position of the Liberal party, if my friends in the far corner would care to examine it, is that, yes, the Liberal party is for a balanced budget in prosperous times and in times of full employment. The same hon. member, after condemning the Conservative government, went on to say this about the Liberals. Referring to our health plan, he said:
I call it now a thorough-going sham and a shameful surrender to vested medical interest, because what does that health plan offer? It offers free health services for the aged, the pensioners. If I remember the words correctly, and I am sure I do, the plan said for some of the aged, and never explained what the word "some" meant. I've always assumed that it meant some kind of means test. It offers free medical service to young people under the age of 16. The rest of the community between 16 years of age and the old age pensioners, if I remember the words correctly, are to pay substantially less than half the cost of the medical services; presumably the government would pay substantially more than half.
The hon. member went on to state the hardship involved in such a plan for a worker who earned $3,000 or $4,000 a year. This statement, again, is of questionable accuracy and it is fortunate that the hon. member qualified his remarks with the words "if I remember the words correctly".
An examination by our friends in the far corner of the brochure put out on health care by the Liberal party would reveal these words. The quotation I am now going to give is referring to all Canadians who are not retired, who are not under the age of 16 and who are not unemployed, who will unquestionably receive the benefits of medicare without any contribution:
For all other Canadians, the plan will cover all doctors' bills above a low annual cost. There will be no charge to anyone who does not go to a doctor. Liberal action will take fear out of health costs. The maximum amount of doctors' bills that anyone will be required to pay will be small; but it will be a safeguard against unreasonable demands for attention.
There, I suggest, is the fundamental principle involved, that the payment contributed by employed persons between the age of 16 and retirement age will be small for the purpose of providing a safeguard only.
The brochure went on to explain how the government would bear the cost and underwrite the expenses of such a program. It is one thing for a party to promote a social welfare program and it is another thing for the party to undertake the responsibility of showing the people how it shall be paid. This latter undertaking by the Liberal party it was, and is, with responsibility and courage, prepared to meet.

How?

It is all in the pamphlet, if you care to read it accurately.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, this is considerably more than can be said for the program advanced by our friends in the far corner, who never quite seem able to meet the added onus of explaining how their programs are to be financed. This same hon. member, presumably referring to the Liberal brochure to which I have just referred, must have been referring to this statement in his comments. I quote from the pamphlet:
They-
"They" is referring to the payments made by individuals for the Liberal health scheme:
They will be designed to cover rather less than a half of the total cost of medical care.
The hon. member for York South did not see fit to quote the sentence immediately preceding that. That statement reads as follows:
How these payments-
Again referring to payments by individuals
-are made will be arranged in agreement with the provinces.
The brochure went on to say that the federal government will pay the rest of the costs from general revenue. For the hon. member to suggest on the basis of such wording that the plan means that a worker earning $3,000 or $4,000 a year would be required to pay half the cost of medical services is a completely unwarranted interpretation. The pamphlet clearly states that with respect to the amount of less than half the cost not incurred by the federal government arrangements will be made with the provinces. How the wording of the brochure could possibly lend itself to the interpretation given by the hon. member for York South is beyond any powers of objective reasoning.
Again, though the hon. member referred to the program as a thorough-going sham and called it a surrender to vested medical interests, it is worth while noting that he did not care to go into the reasoning establishing such a sweeping generalization. By going into these matters, Mr. Speaker, I hope in some degree to have explained with accuracy the program of the Liberal party and, to an extent, to have defended it against baseless attacks.
Some of the comments made by our friends in the far corner-I have referred to several of them earlier, and I shall refer later to others- lead one to wonder whether that group has forgotten that the Liberal party has not been in power for the last five years. At any rate, sweeping generalizations of a condemning nature, together with name-calling depreciations, are always looked upon, fortunately, by the public with a degree of suspicion and

The Address-Mr. Macquarrie on the basis that the program of the government failed to further or enhance the worthy principles which they advocate, but solely on the basis of the political manoeuvring of our Social Credit friends?
Mr. Speaker, it has been enlightening indeed to observe the political gyrations of the N.P.D. up to and after the time of the fateful decision of the Social Credit party. That this house could receive such a lesson in the art of base practical and political manipulation from such a band of idealists would lead one almost to believe that they had feet of clay. Perhaps now that the hem of the white robes of purity of our friends in the far corner is besmirched by the stain of base politics, they can join fully in the deliberations of this "house of sinners".
Mr. Speaker, what I hope my comments have been directed to-and perhaps now our friends in this house, and especially in the far corner, can look constructively and with a long range view at the program of this Liberal party-is to the end of ridding this country of diverse and multitudinous minority groups which, aside from contributing to political and economic instability, are a sign of political narrowness of thought.

To the seconder I extend a particular congratulation because of his felicity in both languages. I have studied French for a great many years and every so often in this chamber I decide that perhaps I will essay forth
[Mr. Munro.l
and speak a few words in French. Then I think how well I regard the French-speaking people and how much I believe in bilingualism. I decide that these feelings could not stand such an assault and I revert again to English. But the seconder set a fine example. I was very pleased, and I wish for him and for the mover a most successful and long tenure in this House of Commons.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to retain my popularity with my colleagues may I call it six o'clock?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, he would be insensitive indeed who did not regard this present parliament at this stage in our country's history as a most significant and momentous assemblage of our nation's representatives. There have been time as I have sat here that I have been filled with feelings of disquiet and I have noted similar feelings have been expressed by some other hon. members. I quite agree with the remarks made by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) this afternoon when he repudiated the suggestion that a "dreary recital of the needs and interests of one's constituency" was not what should be taking place in parliament. Parliament is a place certainly where the cut and thrust of vital debate is exhilarating and appealing and we all enjoy those moments of drama when this intensity takes over.
Parliament is certainly a place for argumentation; but it is much more. It is a chamber for legislation, for deliberation, for that sober and serious reflection and expression of the views and thoughts of the people of the nation. It is not designed for the entertainment of the press gallery. It is designed to express the will of those who have sent us here. If parliament should ever lose its vital ingredient, its representative character, or if that role should fall into disuse, then we can believe that the fundamentals of our democracy are thereby undermined.
I am always interested to hear what the people in the various constituencies have on their minds. We were all enlightened and perhaps a bit horrified by what the hon. member of St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) told us this afternoon. I regret that such a recital had to be made yet I think it was in the interest of strengthening of this parliament that it was made. It is not for me to make

any partisan comparisons but I should like to say that the Leader of the Opposition might well remember the kindly, courteous and generous treatment tat he received at the hands of Premier Shaw of Prince Edward Island. It was a different story there and it always will be a different story because in a free country where political action is free and untrammeled those who seek political office are welcome. We are glad to have people of all parties come to Prince Edward Island. We do not want our people to vote too heavily for some of them but they are welcome and they will be given all the courtesies of free speech. Also, it is not the same in Newfoundland.
While I am disquieted by some of the things which might take place and which might seem to be taking place here, I am sometimes concerned about my own judgment. I thought at one time that the major opposition party was determined to have an election as soon as possible, but when I heard their spokesmen strike out in this direction and then in that direction to castigate their potential allies in any vote in this house, I wondered if I was right in assuming that their intentions were as they are sometimes expressed.
But if there are reasons for disquiet, there are reasons for satisfaction and comfort because I believe that the very closeness of this house is going to save the country. The Canadian people, having seen that the once great Liberal party has come so close to office, are watching as never before its performance in opposition. I think they will look carefully at that apparent lust for power, that desire for immediate possession of office which surely must be the motivation of many of the utterances which we have heard during the election and since the assembling of this parliament.
I thought that in 1958 the decisiveness of the election was caused by the fact that the people were able to compare clearly and vividly the records of the two parties because they could remember the former administration after such a short space of time. Now, happily, this same opportunity for clarity of view has come forward and this is a reason, I think, for comfort to all Canadians. I agree heartily with the last speaker for the Liberal party who spoke about the name calling. I think he is quite right and the Canadian people will depreciate and view with suspicion such tactics. As he is an able speaker, I would suggest that he might perhaps repeat those remarks in his own caucus.
I have noted and Canadians have noted that this intense yearning for office does not express ffself only in the denigration of the
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie Leaders of this country. It will allow itself to go so far as to make expressions and repeated expressions which cannot but diminish their country itself. It pains me that a man of the international repute and prestige of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Green) should have his ceaseless efforts in all parts of the world so castigated and criticized for mere partisan gain. I have seen that man in international conferences. I have heard times without number expressions of the high regard of representatives of other countries. There is much I could say on that matter but I will rest my case very simply on an editorial in one of the great newspapers of the maritime provinces, the Fredericton Gleaner. In referring to his splendid speech at the United Nations general assembly about ten days ago it declared that "the Secretary of State for External Affairs truly represented the Canadian people in his remarks and spoke for us all, as always."
There is another thing that concerns me. I have the honour to represent the cradle of confederation, the city of Charlottetown where in 1864 this nation began. I look upon the development of Canada as a prototype of the development of the commonwealth and I am amazed, a little bit shocked and perhaps a bit amused to discover that, in the tremendous desire to discredit, someone has even picked upon the commonwealth as a part of a strategy to weaken the prestige of the present government and to enhance the fortunes of another political party. It seems to me that the gains which the main opposition party made in the election of June 18-they were significant I must admit, and I would have been happier had they been less-are being overborne by a faulty and unwise strategy. They are going to limit the electoral advances of this party.
Who would have fastened upon the commonwealth as a weapon to belabour the Conservative party? I am not one of those who is a narrow or bitter partisan. I do not believe that any one political party, not even this one away to the right-geographically to the right-has in its bosom all that is good, perfect, wise and profound. But the Conservatives, throughout this nation's history, have been in the very forefront of the development and extension of the commonwealth. It was Sir John A. Macdonald, and I will admit that it was not he alone, who was the founder of this great nation, this assembling of diverse and separated colonies. It was Sir John Thompson who in 1894 brought to this city the intercolonial conference. It was Sir Robert Borden who, though his dogged determination and high sense of Cana-dianism, brought us from the status of a

The Address-Mr. Macquarrie colony to that of a nation and truly earned for himself the appellation of the architect of Canadian nationhood. It was Arthur Meighen who spoke wisely and realistically in 1932 at another imperial conference. I must say to my friends that he was treated as the head of a government should be treated when he was abroad, of course, when he came back he was accused of being a mouthpiece for Washington by the same people who once spoke of him as the lackey of Britain.
It was in 1931, under the government of R. B. Bennett, that the Statute of Westminster became recognized as the charter of our independence. It was in 1932, in this very place, that a great economic conference was held, the fruits of which have a profound effect on our trade pattern to this very day. In 1961, after the commonwealth had grown to include Asia and Africa, after the question of the equality of nations in that commonwealth had long since been disposed of in a large measure through the vigour and wisdom of Conservatives, who gave leadership on that new and important question of the equality of peoples within those nations? It was the Prime Minister of Canada. I would commend to those who seek to advance themselves by denouncing the head of this government, the attitude of the Vancouver Sun, a newspaper which I do not often read and which I do not think is one of ours. They said, speaking of the conference, when it came time for men of courage to stand up and be counted the Prime Minister of Canada was the first man on his feet.
Then, at the commonwealth prime ministers' conference this year, that unique gathering of statesmen of the modern world, who gave leadership? Ask the commonwealth statesmen who were there, or read the communique. Yet, he is criticized, and for what? He was criticized because, sensing the essential nature of the commonwealth, he spoke freely; and as a Canadian he spoke wisely. The commonwealth is an assembly of free nations. It was Borden, many years ago, who stood up and said, "I am always for the British Empire," as it was called then, "but within the empire I am for Canada first. Is that the kind of attitude for which a Canadian statesman should be criticized? I think it would ill-behoove any leader of any party to go abroad and adopt any other attitude. It has amazed me how, in recent months, the Liberal party can be so sure it has all the answers on the question of the European common market, that most difficult, delicate and complex economic assembly. The people of Britain themselves and their leaders are sorely torn as they ponder the proper steps to take at this time. Yet, there are those here who know exactly what Great Britain should do.

I look, too, with pride upon something more that took place at that conference. There was a further extension, as I see it, of this commonwealth ideal, so well nourished and nurtured by Conservative statesmen throughout the years. I refer to the development of a more broadly based trade relationship, centred on the commonwealth but not confined to the commonwealth. This again was a Canadian inspiration by the present head of the government of this country.
I should like to say much more about these things, but there is a question that I have been asked since I have come back to this house. The question is: how is it that in the face of the events of June 18 your province clung so vigorously to the Conservative party? This is a question I am proud to answer. There are many answers, but the overriding one, of course, is that this government has met our needs, has enacted policies for which we have long cried out and which were so long denied. As a former Liberal premier of my province used to say, they never gave the maritimes more than half a deal. I will not weight Hansard with statistics, but I will point out one which is eloquent. In 1956-57 our little province received from Ottawa in conditional and unconditional grants, $5,048,000. Do you know what the figure was in 1960-61? It was $12,491,000. The people of my province are as shrewd and canny, if I may use that island word, today as they were in 1867 when they refused to join confederation until they found it solidly in their interests to do so. When they remembered what was done by some parties, and more significantly what was not done by some parties, they cast their vote as we saw on June 18. This was but one phase of the new measures. I will not call it generosity, I will call it justice, I will call it Canadianism.
We have the same situation in connection with our transportation. Hon. members here know that no Prince Edward Island member could make even a short speech without mentioning transportation. We have now more ferries making more trips and carrying more people than ever before in our history. We are very proud of the fact that we never had such service. We never had so many people coming to our province as we have had lately. Our province has 100,000 people, but this past summer we had a million tourists. A new boat, provided by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) after some nagging by my colleagues and myself, but not too much,-he was very co-operative-moves across the strait from New Brunswick to Prince Edward Island in less than 40 minutes. This is the fastest service on record.

Then someone has mentioned the causeway. I mentioned that causeway a good many times. But we have our commitment in that connection. We were told at the time, as the house records will show, how long it will require for the studies which must precede the eventual construction. I hope that all hon. members in this house will come across that causeway before too long. Just the other day we had the announcement about the Wood island ferry which will tighten the links between my hon. friend from Pictou and myself. It will ply between the two provinces and will be another milestone in the vital field of transportation.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, we were delighted with the ARDA program which will bring some $1,359,000 to Prince Edward Island to develop, expand and improve our basic and oldest industry in our fertile garden province. But one of the things we do not do is dwell in the past, and that is the best of being both a progressive and a Conservative. We are looking forward. The throne speech is filled with forecasts of much sane, sound and sober legislation, but I must say that thing which appeals to me most is the announcement of the establishment of the Atlantic provinces development board. This is something we have sought for a long time.
The government has given attention to our immediate needs through the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, and through increased subsidies; but, as I said in my very first speech in this chamber in 1957, we want an opportunity to help ourselves in the Atlantic region, and this new board will enable us to do that.
A great man in our region, Dr. Wardell, in his convocation address at the University of New Brunswick the other day, centred his remarks on this very item in the throne speech. He said:
We are then, at a turning point in the history of the maritimes. We are about to take a new course which will lead to a fair sharing of Canada's heritage.
I agree with that and I believe the premiers of all the provinces in the Atlantic region agree with it, although I was not quite sure what the premier of Newfoundland meant when he commented on it. The development board is something which we spoke about and sought during our Atlantic province candidates meeting in Charlottetown last spring, and we now applaud the government for its initiative in this regard.
We in Prince Edward Island welcomed the devaluation of the dollar. The hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Smith) has said that the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) helped him during his election campaign by some of the things he has said or written. He
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie helped me also, because when I was trying to convince the electorate that the devaluation was what we needed I could quote from the hon. member for Davenport, and I may say I did. The devaluation of the dollar has had one direct consequence in bringing us the finest tourist season in our history, and it has also helped our two basic industries, agriculture and fisheries. The devaluation of the dollar was a splendid, spirited move which has been economically beneficial to our people. In this connection I was happy to note in today's Toronto Telegram that an outstanding financier, the president of the Toronto-Dominion bank says:
The Canadian dollar crisis is over and while some problems remain to be solved they are not insurmountable.
He went on to say that confidence in the Canadian dollar would continue to grow since the recovery of the nation's foreign exchange reserves.

The people I have the honour to represent have expressed their confidence in the financial and other policies of the government and, as the days lengthen and as time passes in this parliament, I am convinced they will re-ensure themselves in the confidence they have expressed. Like those in many other parts of Canada they will look again at the two great national parties. They will look at the party of which I am a member, which is still the only party with representation from all provinces. They will look at the discharge of its duties in difficult times 

of course we have difficult times in a coum try like this-and I am confident as to the party in which they will place their trust.
Public life is not easy. Indeed it is onerous. Sometimes I suppose we all entertain the thought that it is a little too burdensome. But the thing which prompts me to continue, and comforts me, is that one can see that that part of the country which one represents and loves has had something done for it and its people through the policies of the party he supports.
We in the Atlantic provinces have had qur difficulties. We have had our grievances. The whole subject of maritime plans is pretty hoary now, but never since the far off days of the nineteenth century have we had a government which looked at our difficulties straight in the eye and moved quickly, courageously and effectively to deal with them. It is because of that, and not because of any fondness for the party label, that the Atlantic region has placed its confidence in this government. It is because it has done well for us and by us.

The Address-Mr. Walker

speechtext:
Mr. Deputy Speaker, at the outset I want to congratulate the house on its choice of Speaker when it called upon the man who usually sits in your chair to serve further the interests of our country by acting as our arbiter and as guardian of the moral and spiritual principles upon which our parliamentary democracy rests. I believe I may be forgiven if I make reference to my political ties with Mr. Speaker's constituency of Edmonton West, which he so ably represents.
My interest and participation in politics started in that wonderful and friendly city of Edmonton back in the early thirties when, fresh out of school, I took an active part in the campaign of the Hon. Charlie Stewart, who some hon. members present may well remember. As a boy in Edmonton I earned my pocket money by delivering what has turned out to be a most politically enlightened newspaper, the Edmonton Journal', and not too many months ago I would have willingly distributed that paper without charge.
I also want to thank the Prime Minister for the personal interest he took in my efforts, as far back as July 29 of this year, to have the people of Canada, through the government share the burden and tragedy of the thalidomide babies. There has been some considerable correspondence between the Prime Minister and myself, and it was on his suggestion that I delivered a brief to the deputy minister of health and welfare for consideration when he convened the national meeting of health officials to study the problem.
In these cases the machinery of government never moves fast enough to satisfy a a member who has become personally involved in a human tragedy of the scope and intensity of the thalidomide disaster, and I impatiently wait for the good intentions expressed at the conference of provincial and federal health officials to provide concrete and specific proposals which will relieve the anxiety and heartache of the parents of thalidomide babies. I will not be satisfied, and in this I am supported in a non-partisan way by the three Toronto daily papers, until the federal government assumes the full, final and ultimate responsibility of organizing and putting into effect a comprehensive plan of present care, future rehabilitation and financial assistance for the victims of the drug thalidomide, with or without the participation of all the provincial governments. In this way the Canadian people may be given the opportunity of becoming, as it were, the godparents of the victims of a dominion wide tragedy. This whole affair is too personal a grief for thalidomide families for any party

in this house to attempt to use it in any manner as a weapon with which to pound the government, and I suggest that anyone who would endeavour to do so will bring on himself the disgust of all decent people.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure these remarks will be concurred in by a particular member on the government side of this house and by my colleague from York West (Mr. Kelly), who were ready to accompany me to Ottawa at their own expense in a bipartisan effort to see the Prime Minister and lay before him all the facts. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, I believe the drug companies involved have escaped all too lightly the share of responsibility that may be theirs. As my brief pointed out, in the year ending June 30,	1962 the net profit of
Richardson-Merrell, Incorporated Drug Company rose to $17,250,000 from the previous year's profit of $17,025,000. A substantial annual contribution to assist in relieving the disastrous effects of one of their products, thalidomide, could very easily be set aside from such profits or from their massive advertising budget.
For those in this house who may not be acquainted with the large and vital riding of York Centre which I have the honour to represent, I will simply say that it is the second or third largest by population in the whole of Canada. As well as being part of that lusty giant of a township, North York, which is the largest of metropolitan Toronto's 13 municipalities, York Centre has the good fortune to contain within its borders the historic settlement of Woodbridge, part of the charming village of Thornhill and a large rural area of Vaughan township. So we have a variety of people with diverse interests and backgrounds, and a wealth of human talent which is placed at the service of the community through our many service clubs, church groups and ratepayers organizations.
We are a sports-minded people, and because of the inspiration and splendid example which a certain red-headed member of the Toronto Maple Leafs has provided to the thousands of young people in our minor hockey leagues in York Centre, we are able to completely understand the devotion and loyalty of our Quebec brothers toward that other great Canadian sportsman, Maurice (Rocket) Richard.
Of great assistance to those of us who have lived there longer has been the decisive contribution of vitality to the development and growth of York Centre provided by the thousands of Canadians born abroad, most of them coming to Canada in those good Liberal years. These people have now moved into York Centre and brought with them their great skills and abilities. We need more of them and one can only fervently pray that

one day soon Canada will have an economic policy and an immigration policy that makes it possible for us to welcome many thousands more to this land of freedom.
The particular genius of York Centre's substantial and older Jewish population for scholarship, the arts, professional life and philanthropy has led them to contribute in a measure far beyond their numbers to the cultural life of my constituency. So we are a heterogeneous group, but somehow held together by our common desire to build a better community in our corner of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is not only this minority Conservative government's reputation that is at stake at this time-and believe me, it is at stake-but there is something of much greater importance about which I want to speak, although the government's reputation has a direct bearing on this other matter, and that is the question of the confidence of Canadians in the ability of our free parliamentary democracy to supply the answers and chart the course for the great social changes that are now under way in Canada.
We have not been untouched by the world wide currents of change. Country after country has been caught up in the gruesome side effects of leaderless social revolution, and my major criticism of the government is their failure to recognize and accept the responsibility of providing the courageous and inspired leadership we need if we are to escape the consequences of leaderless change.
It is trite to say we are living in a revolutionary age, but I am not sure that everyone on the government benches, including-especially including-the front benches, realizes what this means in Canada in 1962 and what it will mean in the immediate years ahead. Canada's revolution is still contained inside people; but it is in there, and it is bubbling away and slowly raising the temperature. People are becoming sore and disgruntled, fearful and insecure; the unemployed, the small businessman, the importer, the debt ridden worker, the worried parents of sick children and the pensioner who cannot make ends meet. They want a change and they are determined to get it at any cost. If our parliamentary democracy, Mr. Speaker, will not provide the answers-and I have become convinced it never will, under a Tory government-then our Canadian people may well try some other form of political system in their despair and frustration; and if they do, the failure will be ours.
Mr. Speaker, I would not be sitting in these Liberal benches under the leadership of the next prime minister of Canada if I did not believe that true liberalism is the only political philosophy capable of understanding and leading the social changes that
The Address-Mr. Walker face Canada. My deep conviction is that liberalism, with its concern for the free individual in a free society, is the only safe yet dynamic political ideology for Canada at a time when the unity of Canada is so essential.
Since the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Pearson) took over the leadership of our party, I believe, and I sincerely believe that the greatest thing he has done for all of us and for Canada has been to demonstrate and point the way to the new liberalism adequate to meet the social and economic needs of people in this twentieth century. These are broad new concepts, but on the same bed rock base of principle. We change or we perish. We are a party of change and reform, not chained to doctrine and rigid limitations of nineteenth century policy but ever looking ahead to the solutions of the great social and human problems of our people and mankind.
This man with the incredible courage that only a statesman of his long years of experience could demonstrate has given us all once again a sense of urgency and understanding of the real issues facing us and the hope of an answer. Mr. Speaker, this is why the younger people flock to his side. They can believe him; they can trust him, and they instinctively know this. Our leader will never desert his principles and the principles of twentieth century Liberal democracy in order to win an election or evade an issue. How many times, Mr. Speaker, have you heard people say: "He is too honest to be a good politician"? I tell you this-I would rather lose an election by being associated with an honest statesman whom I can trust to tell me the whole truth than win one by aligning myself with people who constantly deal in half truths, language manipulation and high power propaganda in an effort to confuse and fool the people.
It is no contribution to national unity to hear political leaders in and out of this house publicly intimate that those who disagree with them are either fascists or communists. I can think of no greater tragedy for Canada than that slogans and labels, designed to incite and divide, should be used in place of reasoned argument and enlightened proposals. From personal experience on a municipal council, I know just how hard it is to discipline the tongue but I for one will make an honest attempt in this House of Commons to work at producing unity in the interest of a greater national unity. Surely at this crucial time in Canada's short history when subversive elements of corruption, irreligion and organized disunity are seeping into the lifeblood of our nation, we cannot afford the luxury of

The Address-Mr. Walker irresponsible name calling which contributes nothing to curing the causes of communism and fascism or any other kind of dictatorship.
Our conduct in the interests of a united Canada could give Canadians greater confidence in the ability of free men in a free society to govern themselves. I feel this responsibility deeply, and if I fail at times to adhere to this line it will not be a premeditated political manoeuver but a human failing for which I am sure my friends and especially my opponents will chasten me. These convictions which I have just expressed will in no way deter me from attacking what I think is wrong and fighting for what I know is right.
The proposals put forward in the speech from the throne provide a totally inadequate solution to the urgent immediate problems facing the people of my constituency of York Centre in this year 1962. These 110,000 voters of York Centre voiced their lack of confidence in the ability of the Conservative government to manage the affairs of the country on June 18 last when a previous Conservative majority over the Liberals of 11,000 votes was turned into a Liberal majority of 9,000. I should have thought that this great reversal of public opinion which took place in riding after riding across the country would have jarred the most insensitive government into realizing something had gone wrong. However, instead of applying the lesson to the one place where it would do the most good, namely, to themselves, they decided, through the weird and wonderful process of Tory thinking, that they had received a mandate from a 37.31 percentage of the popular vote to go over to England and in the most shameful way make things as embarrassing as possible for that country in her efforts at economic salvation. The time might better have been spent in the Canadian House of Commons formulating Canadian policies of action designed to produce Canadian economic salvation.
This minority Conservative government stands condemned for its failure to call parliament into session many weeks ago while there was still time to legislate a plan of action adequate to correct the serious crisis of cash and confidence that faces Canada and her people, and while there was still time to legislate a constructive program for those presently unemployed and those about to become unemployed before the dismal months of desolate winter are upon us. My constituents in York Centre do not want to live on unemployment insurance; they want steady work, they want steady jobs, they want to go home at night to their families with the satisfaction of a job well done and a full pay

envelope at the end of the week. The Conservative government cannot much longer withhold from them the opportunity of helping to develop this nation.
This minority Conservative government stands condemned by the manner of their ruthless destruction of that superb, distinctive Canadian achievement of our labour forces, the Avro Arrow. I stood with my wife and little family one Sunday afternoon out in Malton airport watching the test pilot fly the Arrow. That beautiful aircraft was climbing up into the blue skies-

This minority Conservative government stands condemned for its reactionary attitude to any thought of a possible necessity of monetary reform. Of equal importance to the saving of the dollar is the saving of Canada and her people.

This government stands condemned tor its refusal to assume the responsibility of seeing that steady work is available through private or public works for all our people.
This minority Conservative government stands condemned for running the country into the hole, financially, to the point where they apparently cannot produce a co-operative medical care plan for our people.
But mainly, Mr. Speaker, I think this Tory government stands condemned for its failure to have done the long range planning necessary for the successful operation of any efficient business or any prosperous country. What the Tories have been unable to bring themselves to do, we Liberals will do. That is why they are Tories and why we are Liberals. This is a time for decision. This is a time for greatness. The Conservatives have refused to supply it; the Liberals will supply it. The Canadian people have always responded to a call for greatness from an inspired and trustworthy leadership, and they will do it again when given the chance. A call to the hearts and minds of all of us to live for our country, to work for our country, and to sacrifice for our country, would unleash such a response of devotion and true patriotism that Canada would indeed become "the true north strong and free''.
