Mr. Speaker, in offering congratulations to the mover of the address I wanted to say to him that he should forget any embarrassment he felt for the kafuffle in reaching for the motion. I remember my first speech in this house was a situation somewhat parallel to that of the last speaker. I had notes littered all over my desk. There were some fairly sharp people in that house, including the Right Hon. James Gardiner down on the front benches. As I got towards the end of my speech I had my notes all mixed up. So I paused and was reaching and looking for them, which took a fair amount of time, and suddenly out of the chamber came his darting voice: "What are you looking for, boy?-the Regina manifesto?" I can only say that I think I have recovered from that, although it was pretty rough at the time, and I hope the same recovery has already taken place with him.
In offering congratulations to you, Mr. Speaker, and to Mr. Deputy Speaker, I should like to make one observation upon something which has already developed since the day when we met, and that is with regard to the question period. I have always realized, as have most hon. members, that this is very much an informal and unique occasion in parliamentary government. It is really a daily skirmish between the government and the opposition. I think it fulfils the purpose of a commentary on both major and regional problems, and lets the house and the country get some measure of the ministers of the crown. But instead it seems to me that what we may be developing in our question period is a contest between the opposition and Mr. Speaker, and I would only hope that, in the long run, this will disappear and that we will not have a decline in what I think is one of the most important features of our institution. I thought, Mr. Speaker, putting it in colloquial terms, that the last parliament was a lousy parliament in terms of quality, and here I must offer congratulations to all the new members who have come here. I point out especially the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) and the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis), who by the quality of their technique at the very least-if they do not mind my saying this-have certainly heightened and improved this parliament over the last one.
One of the things which is really noticeable in this house, Mr. Speaker, in the debate on the speech from the throne is that the major emphasis has been on economic matters. The paradox that I have found in this, and the major concern that I have encountered among Canadians, is that while economic matters do

The Address-Mr. Fisher concern them, the majority of their concerns are really much wider than that. There is a major frustration. I get it when I talk with businessmen, with housewives, with trade unionists, or with anybody who is within the spectrum encountered by a member of parliament. It usually winds up with this sentence after you have heard their varied complaints: "Why doesn't the government do something about it?" This is not quite as stupid a question as it may seem in our Canadian context, and I should like to illustrate it by giving an example from my own riding and my own region. Our basic wealth producers are pulp and paper, mining, and the transportation industry. Each of these is at the present time fairly sound, relatively efficient, and doing relatively well; but the improvements in these industries over the past decade have given much more productive capacity with either no increase or a drop in the number of jobs provided.
In a nutshell, we are producing more with fewer men. Our service industries have expanded greatly and we have had a fair provision of social capital investment in such things as hospitals, highways and schools. But a relatively small population such as we have can only support so many bowling alleys, motels, curling rinks, drive-in theatres, community television systems and hamburger shops. Our young people are finding it harder to get jobs. The annual incidence of unemployment is creeping up. This is all happening at a time when we have a certain type of affluence. More people have summer camps. There are more winter trips to Florida, more boating, more fishing, much more spending and leisure activities. Thus, at the same time as we have the affluence, we are getting an increasing strain amongst the young people who cannot find a job, and the middle aged ones whose jobs have disappeared or are disappearing. With it all there is a spirit of insecurity and doubt about our own future, and that has tended to permeate our whole region. I think it is just not incidental to my particular region of northwest Ontario.
Several years ago a representative delegation from our part of the country met the minister of labour here to ask for government assistance, specifically regarding winter unemployment, but generally with regard to the rather pessimistic future that seems to face our area. The minister challenged us. He said: "Don't tell me things are bad. I want you to come and tell me why they are bad and what can be done about them." So we took the minister at his word, went home and set up a commission to study the situation and to make recommendations. Last January, after about 18 months work, the commission made


its report and recommendations. These were constructive, limited and realistic. We told the minister why things were bad and we suggested what could be done about them.
Since then we have been on a lovely merry-go-round. Just two weeks ago I finally got a response to the recommendations from the federal Department of Labour. In effect there is not much that the federal Department of Labour can do to help us. In the interim the provincial government has been canvassed and in effect it cannot do very much to help us. The Hon. Robert Macaulay is zooming around Ontario with a zeal not unlike that of his running mate, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees), exhorting us all to buy Canadian, promising drives here and committees there; but in effect he is not accepting very much responsibility for the provincial government for the malaise of our region. We are really back where we started from two years ago. Everyone is concerned but no one is really doing anything effective about it because the lines of responsibility for economic direction in Canada and in our region as a microcosm of Canada are completely blurred.
I should like to point to two federal programs of joint co-operation with the provinces to which I am very partial and our party has been very strong for them. They are the ARDA program and the vocational training program. The acts exist, the money is there but the implementation in a good, sound way always gets fouled up in the question of initiative, jurisdiction and prime responsibility. In brief, we have tentatively crept toward a solution of our goals but we have never climbed over the main barrier to effective co-operation, that is, our divided sovereignties and the fundamental weaknesses of an economy which is plagued with ten different jurisdictions and a host of municipalities and regions complaining and competing with regard to their future and their duties and where they are going.
It is my contention that all our genuflections toward economic planning or a planned economy must be prefaced on securing a recognition of responsibility. We require either constitutional changes or a new flexibility in co-operative programs or goals. As I remarked earlier, the real problems are larger than the economic ones. True, the economy may be the core but the whole apple of problems, it seems to me, is made up of our Canadian nationality, the tremendous interest in education at all its levels, the unease over the inadequacies of our social security, the frenetic dilemma of all our municipalities as they face taxation and financial burdens, the parallel and difficult problem of the family

farm and the family business-has either one any real future?-and the mystery of our defence and foreign policies. All these along with economic problems have created the crisis in confidence that exists in my region, and I would argue in the nation as a whole. In effect, the voters turned us all down last June. Nowhere is this crisis of confidence more apparent, to my mind, than with our political parties.
Before I express my opinions as to our failures as politicians and as political partisans, I should like to underline that our great mistake as a parliament will be that of assuming that the unrest and malaise of our time in Canada are merely economic. We need a coherent series of goals for the nation. These predicate choices that we must make. We must spend a great deal more, not only in money but in thought, on education. We must spend a great deal less on other things by choice. We must do much more to preserve and extend the Canadian identity. Our choice is either that or absorption into the American milieu, both economically and culturally. We must improve our social services by portable pensions, national health insurance and a completely new concept of resolving unemployment through the emphasis and financial support of mobility, retraining and job guidance and testing.
We must strengthen, not weaken, the national institutions which communicate or interpret or develop our culture, such as the C.B.C. and our national press, both daily and periodical. It is really an ultimatum so far as I can see. Either we do this or we are assimilated by a friendly and powerful national consciousness that surges at us from the south. There are so many things I like about the United States that I keep asking myself the question and I want my party to ask the question: Why bother with this damnably indefinite thing, Canadianism? Why not join them? Or if you want to put it in another way, "Is it too late?"
In this kind of dilemma it always seems to me that we have to decide to go for Canadianism. The evangelists, including the previous speaker, are always exhorting us that now is the time for decision. My feeling so far as our national identity is concerned is that this is the time of decision. If we wait much longer we will not have any identity left to preserve. Either we strive much more boldly to develop our institutions in distinction from the Americans or effective assimilation is only a matter of time. We face a choice of whether we are going to be a big country or a small one. The most obvious way for us to become a big nation is to augment our population quickly. This means to me the
The Address-Mr. Fisher choice of a bold immigration policy that will bring millions of people into this country on a staged basis or else we will have a relative decline in the face of both competitors and allies.
Nowhere, Mr. Speaker, can I find a more encouraging approach to our problems from the point of view of total comprehension than in the "Mater et Magistra" document by Pope John XXIII published last year. The quotation I give is concerned with the values and methods of the modern approach to our problems, and it reads as follows:
One of the typical aspects which characterize our epoch is socialization, understood as the progressive multiplication of relations in society, with different forms of life and activity, and juridical institutionalization-
Socialization is, at one and the same time, an effect and a cause of the growing intervention of the public authorities in even the most crucial matters, such as those concerning the care of health, the instruction and education of the younger generation, the controlling of professional careers and the methods of care and rehabilitation of those variously handicapped. But it is also the fruit and expression of a natural tendency almost irrepressible in human beings, the tendency to join together to attain objectives which are beyond the capacity and means at the disposal of single individuals. A tendency of this sort has given life, especially in these last decades, to a wide range of groups, movements, associations and institutions with economic, cultural, social, sporting, recreational, professional and political ends, both within single national communities and on an international level.
It is clear that socialization, so understood, brings many advantages. It makes possible, in fact, the satisfaction of many personal rights especially those called economic-social, such as, for example, the right to the indispensable means of human maintenance, to health services, to instruction at a higher level, to a more thorough professional formation, to housing, to work, to suitable leisure and to recreation.
In this encyclical Pope John raises the question that apparently is overriding my friends directly across the way. The encyclical says:
At the same time, however, socialization multiplies the forms of organization and makes the juridical control of relations between men of every walk of life ever more detailed. As a consequence, it restricts the range of the individual as regards his liberty of action. It uses means, follows methods and creates an atmosphere which makes it difficult for each one to think independently of outside influences, to work of his own initiative, to exercise his responsibility and to affirm and enrich his personality. Ought it to be concluded, then, that socialization, growing in extent and depth, necessarily reduces men to automatons? This is a question which must be answered negatively.
He goes on in this document to point out that there is no need to fear this limitation of the individual, provided we are all aware. I should like to recommend this document to all members of the house, particularly the gentlemen of the Social Credit party who

The Address-Mr. Fisher seem to have a tremendous feeling that the liberty of the individual is going to be interfered with as socialization proceeds.
Another concern I would like to touch upon in this speech is that of parliamentary government. I have expressed the point of view that I thought the last parliament was a poor one. I may say to those members who have asked me whether or not I was going to renew my campaign for improved pay for members of parliament, that I am not. Most of you made me so proud in the last house with the bravery with which you supported me on the floor in connection with that particular matter, that I am going to let the matter drop on the assumption that our need is not as great as that of other people.
The parliamentary system in recent years, Mr. Speaker, has seen the growing power of the executive. I tend to be one of those who believe that this power has become dangerously great. I think there has been a gradual shifting of gravity from parliament towards the professional services of the state. In effect, ministerial responsibility has become a cloak for the lack of effective responsibility of the civil service. The huge increase in administration has not been paralleled by an increase in parliament's capacity to examine and criticize the bureaucracy. There is only time in parliament to air a small fraction of the problems which bureaucracy is involved in, and there is a growing disparity between the knowledge of a parliamentarian and the bureaucracy which has the facts. One commentator has put it this way, a man by the name of R. L. Strauss who has written a book called "The Ruling Servants":
The greatest institutional weakness of parliament as a means of controlling the administration is the fundamental conception of the parliamentary system as the scene of a continuous contest between defenders and attackers of the government. This conception identifies the civil service, as the assumed tool and servant of the political government, with the political self-interest of the majority and compels the minority to formulate every issue in party political terms. Criticism and justification of administrative actions alike thus inevitably assume a political character, and all too frequently cancel each other out without penetrating to the administrative reality behind the parliamentary contest. This deep-seated feature of British par-liamentarianism may also be the ultimate reason for the absence of a specialized committee system which is mistrusted alike by the parliamentary opposition, by the government and, of course, by its official advisers as an encroachment on the rights of the executive.
It seems to me that in Canada this particular refusal of parliamentarians to examine what I think is this problem of parliamentary health is nowhere more apparent than in the first volume of the Glassco commission report which has just come out. This

huge report contains a plethora of recommendations, major and minor, stemming from specific analysis of departments and areas of responsibility; but nowhere is there even a word about parliament's role in the administration, its control or efficiency. You would think the administration was in one limbo and we were in another. I know the excuse is probably that the terms of reference did not allow for this. All I can say is, how can you make a searching examination and effective recommendations on government administration if you do not look closely at the organization that is supposed to be the master of it all? Surely, that is parliament.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me turn to something more avowedly, crassly and enjoy ably political. The other night our rather whimsical Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan), in drawing somewhat sweet conclusions about the high-minded support given the government by the Social Credit, highlighted the bedding together of the socialists and the pseudo-socialists. He read something into this, much as some of us may read something into his gentle wooing of the creditists.
This is a subject worth examination. Just last week one of the authors of the Regina manifesto, Professor Frank Underhill, told me that he felt there were marvellous opportunities in this parliament for the development of a new alignment of the progressive, radical forces in Canada with the Liberals and the New Democrats together-the liberally minded left as he called it. Just before this suggestion was made, I had learned that he had been driven to vote Liberal for the first time in a generation because he thought the present administration so bad.
From another point of view, in my constituency I meet continually Liberals and others who suggest that basically we have so much in common that a means should be found for a constructive co-operation. In order to answer such suggestions and arguments, I find myself at a game one might call pick-apart-the-Liberals. It is a delightfully easy game to play. In my own riding, the Liberals put up a typical new frontiersman. He was handsome, photogenic, desperately anxious to get Canada going again, with lots of money and the very best connections. However, when one examined his political ideas, the new Liberal frontier seemed very much like an old nineteenth century political frontier. This young man affirmed repeatedly that there was no use electing anyone to sit in opposition. It was very clear that the Gallup poll showed the Liberals were going to win. You must have a government member or all was lost. Therefore, you voted Liberal. Now, a lot of people in the riding did vote

Liberal and if they did so, as I believe, because they were taken with this argument, I am taken to the conclusion that the Liberal party is still without a conception of parliament that is democratic and modern. This was one of their bright young frontiersman and this was their line of approach to parliamentary democracy.
Then, there is another aspect of the Liberal party today that needs analysis. My opponent was a young scion of one of Canada's wealthiest families. The other night the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate referred to the government's acquisition of that barefoot boy from Bay street, Mr. McCutcheon. Despite the virtues of noblesse oblige and all that, I wonder what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate thinks about these other people from Bay street or its near environs, such as the impecunious members from Toronto-Davenport (Mr. Gordon), St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Turner) and Vancouver Centre (Mr. Nicholson). Which party came up with the most money to throw around during the last election? Which party do you find the favourite amongst the big businessmen you met? Which party has taken over the Madison avenue type mastery of the slick guff and reiterated banalities, such as the boys of the team jumping off the bus? The answer is rather obvious.
Of course, the Liberal party is riddled with senior administrators, senior civil servants.

A friend of mine who was there said they had a tremendous crowd and before Mr. Pearson's performance the candidate was speaking. He was reading from a text and he reached the stage where he said, "Mr. Chairman, there is one thing I have found as I go around knocking on doors and meeting people in this riding, there is one thing that you need above all"-then he lost his page-"there is one thing you need above all",-and finally he found the page and he said, "patience". This was the best introduction the Leader of the Opposition had during the whole campaign.
The point I wanted to deal with in connection with the Liberal party, one which bothers me, is the outstanding argument that is put forward here by its ablest debaters and which I term the Pickersgill dogma of Liberal administrative genius.

speechtext:
The Liberals have contempt for the new boys, the shaggy fellows on the other periphery of politics. Things were not what they used to be when good old Bud and good old Mitch were deputy ministers. They say to themselves that these new people cannot possibly know the arcana which are revealed only slowly, through imperceptible drops and over long periods, to those who are truly on the inside-the inside with the Liberal party. The senior civil service caste, or the mandarin caste if you prefer, has been allowed to set the tone of the party, and this means worship for the administrative expertise of Mike and Pick and Bud and Walter.
In the abstract sense, essentially liberalism is a creed which preserves permanent values by destructive means. By this I mean that the liberal is always striving to uphold the individual's rights and enlarge the scope of individuality, while striving at the same time to relate these goods to the broader good of society as a whole, and he must suspect anything which does not contribute to these goods automatically. He has not the time for veneration of this or that time-honoured administrative liberal practice. He is or he ought to be right in step with the whole movement of life. He accepts change. He even accepts his ousting from government with a little bit of grace. He tries to guide change or even to anticipate it, and he does this through programs, through legislation and through positive action.
Now if I might skim through the Liberal program.

I repeat that this is nothing more than an argument of administrative genius, but if the Liberal party has this administrative genius and at the same time draws the support of superb fellows like Joey Smallwood, with his economic blackmail to mute rivals, or Ross Thatcher kicking down the doors of empty chambers, surely that is some reason why we hesitate to see this Liberal party as the means for Canada's salvation, as a chance for us to join a party of the democratic left.
Today the fact is that genuine liberalism is called for, but the bitter conclusion I have to reach is that genuine liberalism has been all but stifled in the very party which nurtured it in this country, or claims to nurture it, and which considers itself to have a chance of forming the next government. I cannot give a better example than the dull, uninspiring history of the Liberal party by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and then contrast its dullness and hypocrisy with the wonderful job he did on Mackenzie King and his diaries. In his story of the Liberal party you can see the limitations that are put on a liberal within the Liberal party.
There is no doubt in my mind that, despite the wonderful plea we had this day from the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro), there is not much appearance of genuine liberalism in the Liberal party, and I can say to the Minister of Finance, that funny whimsical fellow who loves these boys across the way, "do not worry too much about this diagonal love affair between the Liberals and the New Democratic party because I have the feeling that they will have to reveal, in this parliament and in their program, much more than just the dogma of administrative genius, or should I call it the dogma of Pick-ersgill's infallibility?

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join my colleagues in offering you my warmest congratulations on your appointment as Speaker of the house. Having been chosen to All this post is a great honour for you and we know that you deserve it because of the work you did here in the past.
I also wish to join the members of this house to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Mr. Speaker, I wish in particular to greet the many young members who, like myself five years ago, made their maiden speech in the house during the last few days. I have noticed also, in the last federal election, that in the Montreal area, at least 19 Liberal mem-

bers were needed to replace one good Conservative member.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, I was listening to the arguments being advanced a few moments ago and I was surprised to notice that these people from the left side of politics, these socialist inclined people, have forgotten their responsibility in this house, the responsibility which was given to them by a colleague of theirs who had courage enough to resign his seat as member of parliament for Burnaby-Coquit-lam. In his direction to the party that former member said he believed a minority government could be a good thing for the people of this country because he believed that a minority government can do more for the people than a majority government.
We have now seen these people turning around and rejecting this sensible policy from one of their former colleagues, and trying to overthrow this government not, as it was said, in the interests of the people but to serve their own political purposes.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, the last federal election has shown that the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) is not the man the Liberal party needs to win in Canada. He has met defeat twice in a row and even if the Liberals show him some consideration by treating him with respect, it is obvious that they have entirely lost confidence in a man who has led them to two consecutive defeats. Dissatisfaction is growing in the ranks of younger Liberals and we would not be surprised if the Leader of the Opposition suddenly took ill and if that pretext were used to replace the present leader of the federal Liberal party by the future leader of the provincial Liberal opposition, Mr. Lesage.
Besides, the Liberals are highly competent as far as Liberal prophecies are concerned. In La Presse of June 13, 1962 there was an article saying:
Lesage predicts Pearson victory.
That is all the competence, the foresight, the accurateness of our friends opposite.
Well, if the Liberals have suffered three defeats since their leader has been in office, they owe it to unreasonable politics, false causes and double dealings.
The Liberal promises during this campaign, Mr. Speaker, we can find in the small textbook, in the bible of the Liberal party published by their own officials and advisers.
This program contains dazzling promises. It mentions an increase of old age pension up to $75; it mentions assistance to widows

and single women as they reach 60 years of age. It contains, as a matter of fact, a whole gamut of electoral promises.
Then there is the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) a new convert to the Liberal cause. I would point out to my friends opposite that when I said the word "convert" I had in mind-let it be said without being disrespectful to the member for Assiniboia- the word "turncoat" that the Liberals change into "convert". According to Hansard of January 23, 1962, the member said:
Canadians have the right to know from what sources will come the amount needed to pay for the numerous and considerable expenses which are announced.
Thus spoke the hon. member for Assiniboia during the debate on the speech from the throne, in 1962.
Well, my Liberal friends, if you want to be logical with your new convert, you had better find out who is going to pay before you make any promises to the electorate. That, Mr. Speaker, is one of the reasons why the leader of the Liberal party was so badly defeated for the third time.
The Liberal vade mecum contains statements which can only bring a smile to the lips of those who are familiar with their platform.
Here is a quotation from page 4 of the Liberal manifesto for 1962:
The Liberal party of Canada favours dynamic good citizenship which will give every citizen the opportunity of fully developing his personality.

Mr. Speaker, I propose to deal tonight with the common market issue because it is a question which concerns not only the members but also all Canadians, the businessmen as well as the workers.
The Conservative convention, which opened today in London will provide for a stormy debate regarding Great Britain's entry into the free trade area of the common market.
Due to the consequences of that issue on the economic future of our country and the subjective stand taken by the Leader of the Opposition in this respect, I believe it is my duty to express my opinion on this matter.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire from the house leader what the business of the house will be for tomorrow, and can the house leader give a projection for next week and tell us what we will be doing then?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I think we will be here next week and for some considerable time. Tomorrow we will consider first the resolution in the name of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, which was introduced today, dealing with amendments to the Export Credits Insurance Act. The second item of business will be the resolution standing in the name of the Minister of Agriculture dealing with amendments to the Farm Credit Act. You will find that is No. 14 on today's order paper. The third item will be second reading of Bill No. C-3, an act to amend the Food and Drugs Act, in the name of the Minister of National Health and Welfare. This is No. 2 on today's order paper. This will be the business for tomorrow and perhaps it will carry over on Monday. It will be possible on Friday, perhaps, to forecast some of the other business for next week.
It being eighteen minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, October 12, 1962
